Pulling it requires per-entry attribution and share-alike awareness; for a private two-user app that is low risk, but it is extra ingestion work. Verify exact fields from /api/v2/schema/ before committing.

claims.claim: Open Workout was not researched (no source gathered).
claims.design_implication: Skip; free-exercise-db plus a small overlay already covers the equipment set.

claims.claim: No open, structured yoga sequencing dataset was found. Search results were only computer-vision pose image datasets (Roboflow CC BY 4.0 for several, a Zenodo 'Yoga for all' set of 10 postures, a GitHub MediaPipe joint-angle set with unverified license). None provides pose-to-pose sequencing or API.
claims.design_implication: Do not generate yoga from a database. Treat Nadia's yoga as a user-chosen session type (duration, focus tags like hips/shoulders/recovery) with templated sequences authored by hand or by the LLM with human review, and log it as a mindful/flexibility workout. Optionally link to her preferred external yoga videos or app.

claims.claim: Hypertrophy volume: Schoenfeld 2017 meta-regression found graded dose-response, growth increasing from 1-4 to 5-9 to 10+ weekly sets per muscle; later work (Baz-Valle) compared 12-20 vs more than 20 with diminishing but gradual returns; a secondary summary gives roughly 4-10 sets per muscle per week as an effective range and a recent meta-regression found frequency matters little once volume is matched. These came through aggregator/blog snippets, not the primary papers.
claims.design_implication: Encode per-muscle weekly set targets as config: roughly MEV about 4-6, working range about 8-16, hard cap about 20 hard sets per muscle per week, starting beginners at the low end. Frequency can be 2x per muscle per week for either a 3-day or 5-day layout. Verify against the primary papers before finalizing numbers.

claims.claim: Double progression, RIR/RPE autoregulation, and deload scheduling were NOT verified from a source in this research pass. They are standard practice and I am stating them from background knowledge: pick a rep range (e.g. 8-12), add reps at a fixed load until the top of the range at target RIR on all sets, then add the smallest load jump and reset to the bottom; deload about every 4-8 weeks or on performance regression, cutting volume about 30-50% at similar or slightly lower load.
claims.design_implication: Implement as deterministic functions in the rules engine with unit tests, and tag these parameters as tunable defaults. Dumbbell availability limits load jumps (unknown dumbbell weights), so ask the user for the actual dumbbell set; with fixed pairs, progress through reps, tempo, unilateral variants, or harder exercise variations instead of load.

claims.claim: Running progression: the '10% weekly mileage increase' rule is weak evidence. A 2008 Groningen study found 20.8% injury in the 10% group vs 20.3% in a 50%-increase group; a 2012 Aarhus novice study found non-injured runners averaged a 22.1% weekly volume increase; a 2018 systematic review (as cited) found no difference between 10% and 24% average increases. Vendor blogs describe adaptive plans that recalibrate from logged runs but those are marketing sources.
claims.design_implication: Use a soft cap on weekly running-volume increases (about 10-20%, with every 3rd or 4th week reduced about 20-30%) plus a single-session cap (e.g. longest run not above about 40-50% of the week). Add guards on spikes relative to the trailing 4-week average rather than treating 10% as law.

claims.claim: Running templates: Hal Higdon 5K Novice is 8 weeks, about 3 runs, 2 strength, 1 cross-train, 3 rest per week (per a TrainingPeaks listing). Higdon Half Novice 1 is 12 weeks, weekday runs 3 to 5 mi, long run 4 to 10 mi. 80/20 (Fitzgerald): about 80% of training at low intensity, 20% moderate-to-hard. Jack Daniels VDOT: a race-performance-derived score mapped to E/M/T/I/R paces; secondhand pace tables vary by source and must be checked against the book or the official VDOT O2 calculator. Couch-to-5K was not researched.
claims.design_implication: Model running as templates (run/walk intervals to continuous 5K to 10K) parameterized by current fitness; use the 80/20 rule to assign intensities (mostly easy). Use Apple Watch workout data (distance, pace, HR) to compute week-over-week adaptation: advance if all key sessions completed at easy effort, repeat the week if one is missed, regress if two are missed or HR drift is high. Do not reimplement VDOT tables from secondhand numbers; compute paces from the published Daniels equations, or use only effort-based (HR/RPE) easy running initially.

claims.claim: Climbing accounting: sources agree climbers overtrain pulling/finger flexors and under-train extensors and antagonists; recommendations include extensor (reverse wrist curl/finger extension) work, daily flexor stretches and tendon mobility, and phasing board/hangboard volume in slowly with off-board rest weeks. No source gave concrete pull-up programming, weekly splits, or hours-between-sessions numbers; the forum source is repeated copies of a single Mountain Project thread.
claims.design_implication: Make climbing a first-class 'external load' session type in the plan: Nick logs climbing sessions (day, duration, intensity) and the engine counts them as high pull/forearm/grip volume. Then (a) remove or cap vertical pulling (pull-ups, rows) and grip-heavy lifts within ~24-48 h of hard climbing days, (b) bias remaining volume toward push, legs, trunk, and shoulder/scapular health, (c) always add small doses of extensor and antagonist work, (d) count climbing finger stress separately and never schedule heavy grip work (deadlift heavy holds, hangs) the day before. Treat the specific hour/volume thresholds as tunable defaults and flag as unvalidated.

claims.claim: LLM-generated programs: the searched literature shows a recurring pattern of LLM generation plus a parsing and validation stage against a schema, retrieval from a curated exercise DB to avoid invented exercises, and sports-science knowledge graphs as grounding. A 2026 repeated-generation study found the same profile can yield structurally different prescriptions across runs, and prior work shows low inter-rater agreement on quality. I found no source evaluating progressive overload logic enforced by a rules engine over LLM output. The commercial WPL 'hallucination-free' claim is unverified.
claims.design_implication: Do not let the LLM own numbers that matter for safety. Failure modes to design against: hallucinated exercises (mitigate by ID-only output constrained to catalog IDs via JSON schema/tool use plus server-side lookup), non-determinism (persist the generated plan, do not regenerate on each view, set temperature low, seed variants), unsafe volume jumps (post-validate weekly-set deltas, load jumps, and running mileage deltas, reject and re-ask with the validator error), equipment mismatch (hard filter candidates before the LLM sees them).

findings.recommended_approach:
Architecture: deterministic rules engine owns the plan, with an LLM used only for choice and explanation within a closed candidate set.

1. Data source. Vendor free-exercise-db (Unlicense, 876 exercises, static JPGs) into Postgres. Add a curated overlay table of roughly 40-80 rows: tags for pull_up_bar, treadmill, mat, climbing-gym; extensor/antagonist and shoulder-health exercises; yoga session templates; fix null equipment rows. Keep a normalized muscle map and movement-pattern tags (horizontal push, vertical pull, squat, hinge, carry, trunk). Optionally enrich with wger names/translations later (CC per-entry license, so skip for now). Per-user equipment profile: Nadia = living room (yoga mat, dumbbells, pull-up bar, treadmill); Nick = those plus apartment gym plus climbing.

2. Rules engine (code, unit-tested, no LLM). Inputs: user profile (level, goals, available equipment, injury flags), weekly availability grid, fixed commitments, recent logs, and recovery signals (Apple Health sleep/HRV/resting HR where available). Responsibilities:
 - Choose split by days available: 2-3 days full body, 4-5 days upper/lower or push/pull/legs plus run/yoga days; 2 exposures per muscle per week.
 - Compute weekly hard-set targets per muscle (beginner low end about 6-10, cap about 20), allocate across sessions.
 - Progression: double progression within rep ranges, with RIR 1-3 targets; load increments from the actual dumbbell set; fallback to rep/tempo/variation progression when loads are fixed.
 - Deload every 4-6 weeks or on trigger (two consecutive regressions, low readiness, missed sessions): cut sets 30-50%.
 - Running: template progression (run/walk to continuous), mostly easy (80/20), weekly volume soft cap about 10-20% over trailing average, step-back every 3rd-4th week, longest run cap, plus miss handling (repeat/regress).
 - Climbing: log as external load; apply grip/pull interference rules and force antagonist/extensor work.
 - Scheduling: constraint solver (simple greedy or CP-SAT/OR-Tools-lite) over a week grid. Hard constraints: work hours, horse days, rest day count, no hard pull after hard climb, no two hard leg/long run days adjacent. Soft: preferred times, session duration fit, spread muscle groups. Re-plan only the remaining days of the week when a session is missed or moved.
 - Fairness: normalize challenge points and targets to each person's own baseline and available time (relative-to-plan completion, effort-adjusted points, time-budget-scaled goals) rather than raw volume, so Nadia's work and horse days don't penalize her. Head-to-head can use percent-of-personal-target.
 - Validators: every plan (human, rules, or LLM) passes the same checks (volume delta, load jump, equipment, rest, running delta).

3. LLM responsibilities (narrow). Given the rules engine's skeleton (session slots, target muscle sets, constraints) and a pre-filtered candidate list of catalog IDs per slot, the LLM picks exercise variety, orders them, writes a short coaching note and rationale, and suggests swaps when a user reports soreness or a skipped exercise. Output is strict JSON with catalog IDs only; server rejects unknown IDs or validator failures and retries with the error message (max 2-3 retries), falling back to a deterministic default pick. Generate once per week, persist, never regenerate on view. Run the LLM from a server job (Claude API or local model is optional; quality not critical because of the validator). Use it also for the periodic 'review' narrative (monthly progress summary).

4. Scheduling around fixed commitments. Store recurring blocks per person (work hours, horse days/times, commute, climbing gym nights) as calendar rules, plus one-off overrides from the app and optionally read Apple Calendar via EventKit on the phone (sync events to server). The scheduler fills remaining free windows, prefers short sessions on work days (20-40 min home/yoga/treadmill, evening), longer sessions on off days. Horse days count as external load (leg/core fatigue, treat as moderate lower-body stress) so the engine avoids heavy leg days adjacent to long horse days. Push the scheduled session to the Watch via WorkoutKit if desired (not verified here).

5. Build phasing. MVP: catalog import, equipment profiles, rules engine with 3-day full body and run/walk progression, logging, no LLM. Phase 2: scheduling constraints and calendar, climbing/horse load, deload logic. Phase 3: LLM for variety/explanations with validators. Phase 4: Health data (HRV/sleep) readiness adjustments.
alternatives: Pure LLM generation per week with schema validation only: simplest to build and flexible but non-deterministic, hard to guarantee progression and recovery; rejected as the core, acceptable as the exercise-choice layer.
Use ExerciseDB hosted API for GIFs and 11k exercises: richer media, but hosted terms, AGPL, and unknown media license plus external dependency; not recommended.

wger as the full workout backend (self-hosted Docker): ready-made logging, routines, and API, but AGPL, Django/Python stack separate from your Go/Next.js choices, and per-entry CC licenses; could serve as reference or data source only.

Adopt existing program templates (e.g. a published 3-day full body or upper/lower beginner programs) as static JSON and only run the progression/scheduling logic; very robust and much simpler, with the LLM limited to swaps. Strong fallback if the generator proves overkill.

Use Apple Fitness+/Strava/Garmin-like adaptive running as the source and only ingest results: removes running logic, but you cannot use their plan APIs (not verified) and it weakens the shared gamification.

verdicts.evidence: The wger README (raw.githubusercontent.com/wger-project/wger/master/README.md) says application code is AGPL-3.0-or-later, exercise/ingredient data is Creative Commons 'see individual entries', and self-hosting is a docker compose away. Latest release is 2.7, published 2026-09-03, and the repo was pushed 2026-10-26. The count the original researcher could not verify is now known: https://wger.de/api/v2/exerciseinfo/?limit=1 returned count 932 without auth, from my environment, using no bot-blocking workaround. I did not re-verify the exercise/exerciseinfo field list, the page size or the throttling claims.
verdicts.correction: Add that exerciseinfo returns 932 entries (one per exercise, with translations nested), which is on the same scale as free-exercise-db. wger is actively maintained, with a release in 2026-09. The 'skip wger for now' recommendation still holds because of the per-entry CC license, but the reason is license bookkeeping, not data quality or maintenance.

verdicts.claim: 6. No open structured yoga sequencing dataset found
verdicts.evidence: I did not repeat the search. The claim is a negative result and cannot be refuted without finding a counterexample. It is consistent with the free-exercise-db finding of no yoga flows.
verdicts.correction: Keep it as 'none found'. The curated yoga session templates in the recommendation are the right fallback.

verdicts.claim: 7. Hypertrophy volume evidence (Schoenfeld 2017 dose-response, Baz-Valle, 4-10 sets/week, frequency matters little)
verdicts.evidence: I did not open the primary papers. Schoenfeld 2017 (J Sports Sci) is a graded dose-response meta-regression with roughly 1-4, 5-9 and 10+ sets/week bands, which matches my background knowledge. The Baz-Valle paper and the 'frequency matters little' meta-regression were not checked.
verdicts.correction: Keep as medium confidence. The planned engine range of about 6-10 sets per muscle per week for beginners, capped at about 20, is conservative and consistent with this evidence. The recommendation does not depend on any single study.

verdicts.claim: 8. 10% rule is weak evidence (Groningen 20.8% vs 20.3%, Aarhus 22.1%, 2018 review 10% vs 24%)
verdicts.evidence: I did not open the sources. The Buist 2008 Groningen trial matches my knowledge: 10% group about 20.8% injury versus about 20.3% in the standard group. The Nielsen 2012 figure and the 2018 review were not checked. The cited sources are Outside Online and a vendor blog, not the papers.
verdicts.correction: Keep the engine's soft cap of 10-20% over the trailing average, but treat it as a heuristic, not an evidence-backed threshold. Note that Buist's comparison group used a roughly 50% week-to-week increase for the first 8 weeks.

verification.revised_recommendation: No refutation changes the architecture. The rules engine owns the plan, the LLM only picks and explains within a validated closed set, and free-exercise-db goes into Postgres with a curated overlay for pull-up bar, treadmill, mat, climbing-gym, antagonist and yoga rows. Three small amendments. (1) The overlay needs about 10 extra rows for pull-up bar tags (Pullups, Band Assisted Pull-Up, Scapular Pull-Up, V-Bar Pullup, Hanging Leg Raise, Hanging Pike and similar), and Finger Curls and the wrist curls can seed forearm and antagonist work. (2) Use the category value 'olympic weightlifting' in the import mapping. (3) wger is a maintained, self-hostable option with 932 exercises and a 2.7 release in 2026-09, but its per-entry CC licensing still makes it a later enrichment. Do not rely on ExerciseDB: its repo has been quiet since 2025-11, its hosted API is rate-limited, and the media and data terms are unread. The volume and running-progression numbers are heuristics from unverified secondary sources. Ship them as configurable defaults, not hard thresholds. This session was in plan mode, so I only ran read-only commands.

findings.topic: Gamification and fair scoring for a two-person couple health app (asymmetric schedules)

claims.claim: Apple Watch competitions score 1 point per percentage point added to the rings each day, capped at 600 per day and 4,200 per 7-day competition. Most points wins.
claims.design_implication: Use percent-of-personal-goal scoring with a daily cap. The cap stops one huge day from deciding the week, and a 7-day duel is a clean unit.

claims.claim: The known weakness of Apple's percent-of-goal model is that the Move goal is user-set. Users report a lower goal earns more points for the same work, and that lowering your goal is the winning strategy. No primary Apple statement found (user reports and third-party blogs only).
claims.design_implication: Do not let goals be freely self-edited. Derive each goal by formula from the person's own rolling baseline, change it only at a fixed cadence (monthly), and show both people's goals to each other.

claims.claim: Duolingo's own blog says streak milestone animations raised 7-day retention for new learners by 1.7%, and allowing up to 2 equipped Streak Freezes raised daily active learners by 0.38% relative. 7-day-streak users are 3.6x more likely to finish a course (not claimed causal). It credits habit formation, loss aversion, and diminishing marginal gain (day 2 to 3 is +50%, day 200 to 201 is +0.5%), and cites research that slack can motivate better than rigid rules. The blog did not cover repair or Streak Society.
claims.design_implication: Make streaks forgiving through banked freezes, not hard-fail. Spend reward effort on early-streak and milestone feedback, and cap the marginal points of long streaks.

claims.claim: The Weekend Amulet was a freeze covering weekend days and was later discontinued (fan wiki). Secondary reports say a 2017 test gave about +4% return after a week and -5% streak loss. A freeze must be equipped before the missed day. Prices and limits vary by source. Perfect Streak Week, special app icons and goal-commitment copy appear in a third-party write-up of Duolingo retention experiments. No primary source found for Streak Society or repair rules.
claims.design_implication: Copy the principle, not the numbers: scheduled rest days (a per-person version of the weekend amulet), pre-banked freezes, and a time-limited repair that costs extra effort.

claims.claim: Strava Relative Effort weights time in heart-rate zones by intensity (TRIMP-like) using the athlete's own max heart rate, so effort is relative to the person; exact coefficients unverified. Garmin Connect weekly challenges rank on raw steps with no handicap (users ask for percent-of-goal). Garmin Auto Goal adapts step goal to history (exact rule unofficial).
claims.design_implication: Score workouts by effort relative to each person's own heart-rate zones, not raw distance or reps. Adapt goals from history. Keep raw leaderboards as non-scoring trivia.

claims.claim: Habitica's rewards depend on task value, difficulty and stats, and its community treats the 'Fix Character Values' escape hatch as legitimate play. Official anti-cheat policy, party/challenge rules and the Finch/Streaks/Way of Life economies were not retrieved (wiki returned HTTP 402).
claims.design_implication: For a two-person honor-system app, make cheating pointless rather than impossible: caps, low weight on unverifiable items, and a visible correction path. The point-economy comparison with Finch, Streaks and Way of Life still needs a follow-up pass.

claims.claim: BE FIT (JAMA Internal Medicine 2017) gave families 70 points per week, losing 10 on days the step goal was missed, and reached goals on 0.53 of days vs 0.32 for controls. In iDiabetes (JAMA Network Open 2021), gamification with support and gamification with competition both increased steps vs control, while a collaboration arm with strangers did not. Read from news summaries, not full text.
claims.design_implication: A weekly point bank that erodes on missed days is a validated, cheap commitment device. Use it for the shared household pool, alongside both competition and partner support.

claims.claim: A 2022 JMIR randomized trial of 20-day step incentives found financial incentives beat control, but deposit contracts (loss framing) were no better than plain rewards, had lower uptake (about 62% vs 100%), and loss framing reduced effectiveness in healthy adults. The authors flag limited power.
claims.design_implication: Do not rely on punitive loss mechanics. Use loss aversion only through streak and banked-point erosion, with mild penalties and rewards as the main driver.

claims.claim: Cooperative goals produced more reported effort than competitive ones in a game experiment. A 2024 study found competition raised performance but also lasting physiological stress, so cooperation may be better when wellbeing matters. A basketball study found no difference. A 2026 VR study says competitive exergaming raises intensity but some users have a worse experience depending on competitiveness. Evidence is on strangers, students or games, not couples.
claims.design_implication: Make cooperative goals the spine and the duel a light weekly layer. Let either person dial the head-to-head down.

claims.claim: Kohler motivation gain: a preregistered meta-analysis of 19 articles found a significant motivation gain for partnered exercise vs alone. Plank studies with virtual partners show gains, and a summary of a bike study says the weaker member gains most from a moderately stronger partner. No study of romantic couples or of competition inside couples was found. A 95-person daily-diary study found exercising with a partner raised positive affect and relationship satisfaction that day (correlational), and a 2026 review calls the evidence mixed.
claims.design_implication: Reward doing things together (a joint workout or cooked meal earns a shared bonus), and show a reachable gap to your partner. The evidence supports partner presence more than scoreboard rivalry.

findings.recommended_approach:
Proposed scoring model (my design built from the sources; formulas are my inference, not published anywhere):

1. Personal goals by rule. Target T(p,h) = clamp(median of p's last 4 weeks of actuals x 1.05, floor, ceiling); floor and ceiling agreed once by both; recomputed monthly only. Availability scaling: each week each person marks work hours, horse days and travel. Capacity c = free_minutes_this_week / personal_median_free_minutes, clamped to [0.6, 1.2]. Effective target T_eff = T x c. Schedule load lives in the denominator, so neither person has an edge from free time and nobody can lower a goal by editing it. Show both people's targets and capacity inputs to each other.

2. Daily habit score s(p,h,d). Continuous habits (steps, run km, active minutes, audiobook minutes, home-cooked meals): s = min(1.25, actual / T_eff). Binary habits (teeth AM/PM, creatine, Huel, sleep window): s = 1 if done. Workout actual = effort units from heart-rate zone minutes weighted by zone, using that person's own max HR (Strava-style). Beyond 1.25, nothing further (cap as in Apple).

3. Daily points = 100 x sum over h of w_h x s. Starting weights: movement 0.25, workout or run 0.20, nutrition (home-cooked, no delivery order) 0.20, sleep 0.10, basics 0.10, reading or audiobook 0.10, screen time 0.05. Screen time is scored as a ratio to own 4-week baseline.

4. Weekly duel. WeekScore(p) = sum of the 7 daily points, with each day capped. Winner = higher WeekScore. Tie-break and a secondary badge go to the bigger improvement: z = (WeekScore - mean4) / max(sd4, 0.1 x mean4). A separate non-scoring Hall of Fame tab shows raw totals (most pushups, most miles) for bragging.

5. Cooperative layer (primary). Household streak: a day counts if both reach at least 70% of their own daily target. Weekly shared quests (cook at home 5 dinners, both run 3 times) with team progress = min of the two. Joint bonus +10 each for logged-together workouts or meals. Points above 70% of target feed a shared date-night fund. Weekly winner picks the weekend meal or movie, so a lopsided duel never costs the loser anything real.

6. Streaks. Per-habit and household; a day counts at s >= 0.7. Up to 2 pre-declared rest days per person per week never break a streak (weekend-amulet analog). Earn 1 freeze per perfect week, bank up to 2, applied automatically. Repair within 24 hours by earning 1.5x the daily goal, once per month. Milestone feedback at 3, 7, 14, 30, 60 days with the largest reward early. Streak bonus capped at about +10%. Loss aversion through a weekly point bank that erodes slightly on missed days (BE FIT style), no deposits or penalties.

7. Anti-gaming. Prefer HealthKit sensor data and treat user-entered records as low trust. Per-habit caps with diminishing returns, and a combined weight cap for self-report-only habits. Food logging rewards logging and cooking at home, never low calorie totals (my inference, to avoid pushing disordered eating). Partner can flag a suspicious entry, and an edit-with-reason correction path exists (spirit of Habitica's accepted Fix Values).

8. Rewards. Badges, a year-long start-vs-now metrics page, date-night fund, winner picks weekend meal, loser picks the next activity, quarterly bigger reward agreed together. These are unsourced choices for low cost and low friction.
alternatives: Pure Apple-style percent-of-ring scoring with fixed agreed goals: simplest, but invites the lower-your-goal exploit.
Fully cooperative mode with no duel: best wellbeing evidence, but drops the pushups-and-miles rivalry Nick wants.
Handicap or Elo-style duel against expected score from own history: statistically fairest, harder to explain and tune for two users.
Time-budget normalization only (points per available hour): directly addresses job and horse schedule, but needs reliable schedule input and could reward under-using free time.
Heart-rate effort scoring only (Strava or TRIMP style): fair across fitness levels, but ignores non-workout habits like teeth, creatine and reading.
cannot_do: Verify Duolingo Streak Society, streak repair rules or Weekend Amulet figures from a primary Duolingo source; only fan wiki and third-party summaries were found.
Find any study of competition between romantic partners; the evidence is on strangers, students and games, so all couples conclusions are inference.
Retrieve Habitica's official anti-cheat policy, party and challenge rules or reward formulas; nothing on Finch, Streaks or Way of Life point economies was found.
Verify Strava's Relative Effort coefficients or Garmin's auto-goal rule from official docs.
Read the full text of BE FIT or iDiabetes; those facts come from news summaries.
Research Stridekick or Fitbit challenge rules; not covered.
Confirm the weights, caps and 0.7 threshold; they are untested starting values.
open_questions_for_user: How competitive are each of you really, and does Nadia want a head-to-head at all or a cooperative-first experience with a light weekly duel?
Should availability scaling be automatic (calendar plus HealthKit) or a quick manual weekly check-in?
Should nutrition points reward only logging and home cooking, not calorie targets?
What rewards would you both actually care about, and who controls payout?
Do you want raw leaderboards (most pushups, most miles) visible at all?
How strict should self-reported items be: pure honor system or a partner-verification step?

verdicts.claim: 1. Apple Watch competitions: 1 point per percent of ring, 600/day cap, 4,200 per 7-day, most points wins
verdicts.evidence: Apple support page fetched (https://support.apple.com/guide/watch/compete-with-friends-apd68a69f5c7/watchos) states 1 point per percent added to rings, up to 600/day, 7 days, 4,200 max, most points wins. Search found no watchOS 26 change, but the cached/localized pages seen were older versions, so iOS 26 non-change is unverified.
verdicts.correction: None needed on the numbers. Note that the current-version page fetched matches; no evidence of a watchOS 26 change.

verdicts.claim: 2. Weakness: user-set Move goal means a lower goal earns more points; no primary Apple statement
verdicts.evidence: Third-party sources (iDropNews https://www.idropnews.com/news/apple-watch-activity-competitions-are-rigged-but-apple-can-fix-it/125310 and Macworld https://www.macworld.com/article/673405/how-to-set-up-and-win-apple-watch-competitions.html) make the same point, and Macworld advises syncing goals before a competition. Logically follows from the 1 point per percent rule. Apple has no primary statement.
verdicts.correction: None. Add Macworld as a source. I did not open the two originally cited Apple Discussions and Podfeet URLs, so those are unverified by me.

verdicts.claim: 3. Duolingo blog statistics (+1.7% 7-day retention, +0.38% DAL for 2 freezes, 3.6x course completion, 50% vs 0.5% diminishing gain, slack research, no repair/Streak Society)
verdicts.evidence: Fetched https://blog.duolingo.com/how-duolingo-streak-builds-habit/: +1.7% 7-day retention for new learners from the animation, +0.38% relative DAL from equipping up to two Freezes, 3.6x as likely to complete course at a 7-day streak, 2 to 3 days = +50%, 200 to 201 = +0.5%, cites a UPenn/UCLA study that slack can motivate more than rigid rules, and does not mention repair or Streak Society.
verdicts.correction: None. The 'loss aversion' and 'habit formation' attributions were not individually re-verified in my extraction.

verdicts.claim: 4. BE FIT (JAMA IM 2017) 70 points/week, -10 on missed days, 0.53 vs 0.32 goal days; iDiabetes (JAMA Netw Open 2021) support and competition increased steps, collaboration with strangers did not
verdicts.evidence: Search summaries: BE FIT is Patel et al., JAMA Intern Med 2017;177(11):1586-1593, 70 points per week per family, 10 lost on days the step goal was missed by the randomly chosen family representative, proportion of days goal met 0.53 vs 0.32. iDiabetes (Patel et al., JAMA Netw Open, May 2021, 361 adults with T2D, four arms): support about +503 steps/day, competition about +606, collaboration +280 (95% CI -115 to 674, P=0.16, not significant). Sources: https://pennmedicine.org/news/news-releases/2017/october/to-increase-exercise-study-shows-gaming-strategies-and-a-buddy-are-key, https://pennmedicine.org/news/news-releases/2021/may/game-based-program-boosts-physical-activity-among-diabetes-patients. Direct fetches of both Penn URLs returned 404 today, so the press pages may have moved; verification came from search snippets of those pages and others, not the full texts.
verdicts.correction: Add that BE FIT is families in the Framingham Heart Study (not couples per se) and the loss was applied when the representative missed the goal. The iDiabetes participants were adults with uncontrolled T2D, and weight/HbA1c did not differ from control. Penn URLs now 404; cite the journal DOIs instead.

verdicts.claim: 5. 2022 JMIR trial: incentives beat control; deposit no better than reward; uptake about 62% vs 100%; loss framing reduced effectiveness; limited power
verdicts.evidence: de Buisonjé et al., JMIR 2022 (https://jmir.org/2022/10/e38339/PDF; abstract mirror https://pure.eur.nl/en/publications/investigating-rewards-and-deposit-contract-financial-incentives-f/): incentive conditions met goal on mean 13.10 days vs 8.00 control (p=.002); deposit uptake 61.7% vs 100% for rewards; authors conclude deposits were not more effective than rewards and that loss framing was less effective than gain framing. Design: 126 healthy young adults, 2x2 (deposit vs reward, gain vs loss feedback) plus control. Power caveat appears in the search summary of the paper; not seen in the abstract text I fetched.
verdicts.correction: Clarify that 'loss framing' was the feedback frame (a 2x2 factor), separate from deposit vs reward. The participants were healthy young adults, and the deposit-vs-reward difference was not significant (14.88 vs 12.13 days, p=.166, per search summary).

verdicts.claim: 6. Cooperation vs competition evidence: 2012 game experiment, 2024 physiological stress study, basketball no difference, 2026 VR exergaming study; evidence not on couples
verdicts.evidence: PMC11263633 is De Francesco et al., iScience 2024 (VR Stroop task, 50 and 58 participants): competing against a higher performer raised perceived stress and heart rate, and the stress persisted over blocks; but cooperation with a lower performer produced comparable accuracy, and the study had limits (single task, heart rate alone ambiguous, 'cooperation' was team vs team). Frontiers in VR 2026 (frvir.2026.1897543): 30 people, single session, within-subject; AI-competitive gave highest power (147.0 W vs 140.2 cooperative vs 127.1 solo) and highest HR; cooperative-framed had highest enjoyment; a few found the target pressuring; the paper did NOT analyze by competitiveness (no competitive-orientation measure) and the competitive condition used HR-responsive pacing, a confound. I did not open the Wei 2012 or ResearchGate basketball sources.
verdicts.correction: The 2024 study is about a Stroop task with a virtual agent, not a performance-and-wellbeing study of exercise, and the 2026 VR claim that 'some users have a worse experience depending on competitiveness' is not supported: the paper did not measure competitiveness; it only reports a few participants finding the pace target pressuring. Reword to: competitive framing raised intensity in a small 30-person confounded study, cooperative framing had the highest enjoyment.

verification.revised_recommendation: The scoring design survives intact. Changes: (a) Keep the cooperative-primary, light-competition layer, but justify it from the iDiabetes result (competition and support both worked; collaboration among strangers did not, which does not apply to a couple) and from enjoyment/stress data, and drop the claim that research shows competitiveness moderates experience. (b) The no-deposit, no-penalty choice is well supported: deposit uptake was only 61.7% and deposits were no more effective than rewards, and loss-framed feedback did worse than gain-framed feedback in healthy adults, so favor gain-framed feedback and treat the BE FIT-style eroding point bank as optional and mild (BE FIT's lost points applied to the family, was a different population, and the claim is not a general result about loss framing). (c) Rely on rule-derived personal targets rather than user-set goals, since Apple's percent-of-goal model rewards low goals (confirmed by third-party sources, no Apple statement). (d) Streak design (freezes, early milestones, diminishing returns) is supported by the Duolingo blog numbers, but those are Duolingo's own A/B results on language learners, so treat repair and the 70% threshold as untested design choices. (e) Cite journal DOIs rather than Penn press URLs, which now 404."

findings.topic: Automatic reading and audiobook progress tracking on iPhone (Audible, Apple Books, Libby, Audiobookshelf, Hardcover, Kindle, Shortcuts fallback)

claims.claim: Audiobookshelf (ABS) is the only source with a documented, official, per-user API for progress, sessions and stats. Auth is a per-user API token sent as Authorization: Bearer (query ?token= also works on GET). The API reference lists: Get Your Listening Sessions, Get Your Listening Stats, Get a Media Progress, Create/Update Media Progress, Get Library Items In Progress. Media progress fields: currentTime, progress, duration, isFinished, lastUpdate (ms epoch), startedAt, finishedAt, hideFromContinueListening.
claims.design_implication: Run ABS in the same Docker stack. The Go backend polls each user's /api/me endpoints (sessions, stats) every few minutes with each user's token and converts new listening time into points. Exact response schemas for sessions/stats were not read (the fetched docs page was truncated); confirm against a live instance.

claims.claim: ABS listening sessions carry duration, time listened and current position but no finished flag. Finished state lives on the media progress record (auto-set when remaining time is under the markAsFinishedTimeRemaining setting, default 10s). Ebook reading in ABS creates no sessions.
claims.design_implication: Use sessions (timeListening deltas) for minutes-listened scoring and media progress for book-finished bonuses. Do not try to score ebooks via ABS. Source is a single user's issue report, so verify on a live instance.

claims.claim: The official ABS iOS app is still an early beta distributed only via TestFlight (limited slots, reported full). Third-party iOS clients exist: ShelfPlayer, Plappa, Still, Prologue, SoundLeaf. ABS docs warn that some third-party apps use endpoints no longer recommended, which can produce incorrect sessions and stats.
claims.design_implication: Pick one third-party client (ShelfPlayer or Still were the ones stating session/progress sync) and test that it creates proper sessions, including offline playback that syncs later. Reliability as a progress source depends on the client choice, so test before committing. I did not verify offline-sync behavior of any specific client.

claims.claim: ABS only helps for audiobooks you own as files. It cannot play Audible or Libby DRM content directly. Audible books can be brought into ABS via Libation or audible-cli (download and strip DRM), which is a legal gray area but low risk for personal use.
claims.design_implication: Decide whether you will move listening into ABS (high automation, extra effort of ripping/buying DRM-free) or stay on Audible (lower automation). Libation and OpenAudible were not fetched; their purpose (library download/export) is from background knowledge, and neither is known to expose listening progress.

claims.claim: Audible has no official public API. The unofficial Python library mkb79/audible (and audible-cli, a CLI on top of it) authenticates as a device and calls private endpoints. GET /1.0/library with response_groups can return listening_status, percent_complete and is_finished. GET /1.0/stats/aggregates returns daily listening for up to 30 days and monthly for up to 12 months. A per-book last position exists but not a history.
claims.design_implication: A Python or Go sidecar (cron) could poll each person's Audible account every 15-60 min and derive listening minutes from percent_complete or position deltas times duration, or from stats/aggregates. This is brittle (private API, auth can break, ToS gray area, field name last_position_heard is unverified). Treat as an optional bonus source, never the only one. Needs a one-time device-registration login per person.

claims.claim: Libby/OverDrive has no public API for individual users and no listening-progress export. Libby has an Activity Timeline (checkouts history) that can be exported only as part of locally stored data for troubleshooting. Progress sync is not documented in any source found.
claims.design_implication: Do not build automation for Libby. Libby listening is manual or Shortcut-timer only. Nothing about an unofficial Libby API was verified, only that none was found.

claims.claim: Hardcover.app has a public GraphQL API at https://api.hardcover.app/v1/graphql. Token comes from hardcover.app/settings and is sent as a Bearer header. Reported limits: 60 requests/min (burst 10, ~5000/day per one developer's header measurements), 30s timeout, max query depth 3, each top-level field costs a request, user_book_reads row cap 1000. user_book_reads has progress, progress_pages, started_at. Mutations exist: upsert_user_book_reads, insert/update_user_book_reads, plus user_book status changes.
claims.design_implication: Hardcover is a good book-level source (currently reading, finished, ratings, shelves, yearly goal) that both users could keep in sync with ABS (ABS community integrations exist) or manual updates. Poll hourly or less, which is far below limits. It records page/percent and finish dates, not minutes read, so score on finished-book events and progress deltas. docs.hardcover.app returned 403 to WebFetch, so exact auth header and current limits should be re-verified in a browser. From memory (low confidence), tokens may expire and need periodic re-issue.

claims.claim: StoryGraph has no public API and Goodreads closed its API to new developers in 2020. Both offer CSV export (StoryGraph from account settings; Goodreads from My Books > Import/Export) and Goodreads RSS feeds of shelves, though these are less reliable now.
claims.design_implication: Not researched this session (no source fetched), so this is from background knowledge. Skip both and use Hardcover, which has a real API. Only revisit if one of you already tracks books in StoryGraph.

claims.claim: Apple Books exposes no reading progress or session data to Shortcuts or to third-party apps. Apple documents only Reading Goals and iCloud progress sync for users. The .books App Intents schema is for third-party ebook readers to expose their own actions. Screen Time per-app or per-category usage is not readable by a normal app: DeviceActivity/FamilyControls is privacy-restricted (the app can only react to thresholds and render a report extension, not receive raw numbers), and the FamilyControls entitlement needs Apple approval.
claims.design_implication: No automation for Apple Books. The Screen Time statements are from background knowledge, since the search returned nothing on DeviceActivity; verify in Apple docs before designing screen-time-based scoring. A Shortcuts timer or manual log is the Apple Books path.

claims.claim: Kindle has no public API or export for reading progress. Whispersync data only reaches Amazon servers. Scraping read.amazon.com (cloud reader) was tried by others and described as hacky, and likely violates Amazon ToS. The 2026 Kindle iOS app reportedly has Goodreads integration and real page numbers.
claims.design_implication: Do not scrape Kindle. If either of you reads on Kindle, use manual minutes or Shortcut timers. Goodreads sync is not a useful ingestion path since the API is closed.

claims.claim: iOS Shortcuts Personal Automation supports an App trigger with Is Opened and Is Closed, and the Run Immediately option skips the confirmation prompt. An automation can then run Get Contents of URL (HTTP POST) to the server. Apple's user guide confirms app-opened triggers and run-immediately in general. An explicit statement of Is Closed plus Get Contents of URL working unattended was not found in the sources fetched.
claims.design_implication: Create two automations per audiobook/reading app (Opened posts start timestamp, Closed posts end). The server pairs them into a session and caps/validates it (e.g. ignore sessions over 3h, since app-open does not mean actively listening, and audio apps keep playing after being closed from the switcher). Needs a one-time on-device test per phone. Risks: backgrounded audio apps may not trigger Closed; the user has to set up the automations themselves (cannot be shipped in the app). Shortcuts can only be installed per phone by the user or via an iCloud shortcut link.

claims.claim: A native in-app timer or manual log can write to Apple Health as Mindful Minutes (HKCategoryTypeIdentifierMindfulSession), and the Apple Watch Mindfulness app also writes that type, but Health data has no concept of reading vs meditation. Using Mindful as a reading signal conflates the two.
claims.design_implication: Prefer an in-app Reading/Listening timer (Start/Stop, optional Watch complication) that posts directly to your backend and tags the source (book, audiobook). Skip HealthKit Mindful for reading. Based on background knowledge, not fetched this session.

findings.recommended_approach: Layered approach, ranked by automation level per source. (1) Core, fully manual-reliable: an in-app Start/Stop timer plus quick 'I read/listened N min' log (tagged audiobook/ebook/paper, optional book title) that posts to the Go backend. This works for Apple Books, Kindle, Libby, Audible, paper books and is the guaranteed fallback; award points for minutes with a daily cap. (2) Highest automation for audiobooks: self-host Audiobookshelf in the same Docker Compose stack, use one ABS user per person, and have the backend poll each user's listening sessions/stats/media progress with their token. Pair with a vetted third-party iOS client (ShelfPlayer or Still; test offline sync). This gives hands-off, per-user, minute-accurate data and finished events, but only for audiobooks you can put in ABS (DRM-free files or ripped Audible via Libation/audible-cli). (3) Book-level metadata: Hardcover GraphQL for currently-reading, finished, ratings and the yearly reading goal, polled hourly, optional per person. (4) Optional best-effort: Audible via the unofficial mkb79/audible library sidecar polling library percent_complete and stats/aggregates, marked experimental and nonessential. (5) Optional low-effort automation: Shortcuts personal automations (App Is Opened/Closed, Run Immediately, Get Contents of URL) for apps with no data source (Libby, Kindle, Apple Books), with server-side session pairing and caps; treat as unverified until tested on both phones. Anti-cheat is light: caps per day and require both open and close events. Automation levels: ABS high, Hardcover medium (events, not minutes), Audible medium-low (brittle), Shortcuts medium (approximate), Libby/Kindle/Apple Books none beyond the manual timer or Shortcut.
alternatives: Skip Audible/Libby/Kindle entirely and go all-in on ABS plus Hardcover: simplest and most robust, but forces DRM-free audiobook sourcing.
Manual timer plus Shortcuts only: zero third-party dependencies, least accurate, relies on discipline.
Use Hardcover alone (finished books and pages) and score per book/page rather than minutes: very low maintenance, coarse granularity.
Run Libation to auto-rip Audible to files and sync into ABS so Audible stays the purchase source and ABS the listening source.
cannot_do: Read Apple Books reading progress or time automatically through any public API or Shortcuts action.
Get Libby/OverDrive listening progress or minutes programmatically; no public or documented user API found.
Read Kindle/Whispersync progress without scraping or unofficial endpoints; no export exists.

Read per-app Screen Time minutes (e.g. Books or Audible) from your own app; DeviceActivity is privacy-restricted and gated by a FamilyControls entitlement (from background knowledge, unverified here).
Ship Shortcuts automations inside the app; each user must create them on their own phone.
Guarantee that an 'app closed' Shortcut fires when an audio app keeps playing in the background; not verified.
Rely on the Audible unofficial API long term; it is undocumented and can change or break auth at any time.
Verify StoryGraph and Goodreads options in this session; no sources were fetched, so those are unverified background claims.
open_questions_for_user: Where do you each actually listen/read today: Audible, Libby, Apple Books, Kindle, paper? Roughly what share is audiobooks?
Are you willing to move audiobooks into Audiobookshelf (DRM-free files or ripping Audible with Libation), or must listening stay in the Audible/Libby apps?
Should reading points be based on minutes, pages/percent, or finished books, and should ebook minutes count equal to audiobook minutes?
Do either of you already use Hardcover, StoryGraph or Goodreads, or would you start Hardcover fresh?
Are you comfortable creating a few Shortcuts personal automations on each phone, or should the app avoid any manual iOS setup?
Is the Audible private API ToS gray area acceptable for a personal sidecar, or do you want to avoid it?
Does a time cap per day (e.g. 90 min counts) fit the fairness rule given Nadia works full time and you work from home?

verdicts.claim: 1. ABS has a documented per-user API (Bearer token, ?token= on GET); endpoints for sessions, stats, media progress, in-progress items; progress fields listed.
verdicts.evidence: https://api.audiobookshelf.org/ confirms Bearer header and ?token= on GET, and lists Get Your Listening Sessions/Stats, Get a Media Progress, Create/Update Media Progress, Get Library Items In Progress. Progress fields id, libraryItemId, duration, progress, currentTime, isFinished, hideFromContinueListening, lastUpdate (ms), startedAt, finishedAt all appear. Not verified: the 'only source' wording.
verdicts.correction: Soften 'only source' to 'the only source with a documented official per-user API among those evaluated' (Hardcover also has a documented API). Also available: Get a User's Listening Sessions/Stats (admin), Batch Update Media Progress, Sync Local Sessions.

verdicts.claim: 2. ABS sessions have no finished flag; finished lives on media progress (markAsFinishedTimeRemaining default 10s); ebook reading creates no sessions.
verdicts.evidence: Could not verify against primary docs in this pass (docs.audiobookshelf.org had a certificate error; only the API reference was readable and its excerpt did not cover the session schema). The cited source is a third-party GitHub issue.
verdicts.correction: Treat as plausible but unverified. Before relying on it, check the session schema at https://api.audiobookshelf.org/ and the finished threshold in a live instance.

verdicts.claim: 3. Official ABS iOS app is early beta on TestFlight (reported full); third-party iOS clients exist (ShelfPlayer, Plappa, Still, Prologue, SoundLeaf); docs warn some third-party apps use discouraged endpoints.
verdicts.evidence: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/advplyr/audiobookshelf-app/master/readme.md says iOS is early beta and the TestFlight beta is full (Apple's 10k cap). Search results confirm third-party App Store clients: ShelfPlayer, AudioBooth, Audiary, SoundLeaf, Prologue (https://www.iphone-ticker.de/hoerbuch-app-prologue-unterstuetzt-jetzt-auch-audiobookshelf-server-271074/, https://terminalbytes.com/soundleaf-ios-client-audiobookshelf-launch). The endpoint warning on the community-apps page could not be fetched (certificate error), so it is unverified.
verdicts.correction: The roster is larger and changing (AudioBooth, Audiary are also listed). Plappa and Still were not independently re-checked. The readme gives no 2026 status update, so confirm the beta state on Discord. Pick the client by testing offline sync and session reporting against your own server.

verdicts.claim: 4. ABS only helps for DRM-free files; it cannot play Audible/Libby DRM; Libation or audible-cli can strip Audible DRM (gray area).
verdicts.evidence: https://github.com/mkb79/audible-cli shows it decrypts AAX/AAXC files and has an `api` command for raw Audible API calls, which supports the audible-cli part. Libation is not mentioned on that page. The legal-risk judgment is the researcher's opinion, not a sourced fact. Libby/DRM non-playback was not checked.
verdicts.correction: Keep as 'audible-cli can download and decrypt Audible books for personal backup; legality varies by jurisdiction and Audible terms'. Drop 'low risk' as an unsupported claim.

verdicts.claim: 5. Audible has no official API; mkb79/audible and audible-cli call private endpoints; /1.0/library gives percent_complete/is_finished; /1.0/stats/aggregates gives 30 days daily and 12 months monthly.
verdicts.evidence: https://github.com/mkb79/audible-cli is active (287 commits, a Rust rewrite in progress, and a note that old download names are dropped after 15 November 2026), and it exposes raw API calls. The specific endpoint fields and aggregate windows were not verified from a primary source.
verdicts.correction: Treat the field names and windows as unverified. Probe a real account with `audible api` before designing around them. Note that the audible-cli project is mid-rewrite, so it carries churn risk.

verdicts.claim: 6. Libby/OverDrive has no public per-user API or progress export; Activity Timeline is exportable only as local troubleshooting data.
verdicts.evidence: No primary source was fetched for this claim. The cited sources are a library knowledge base and a 2017 OverDrive blog post, which are old and secondary.
verdicts.correction: Keep as 'no known public API or progress export' (negative claim, low-to-medium confidence). Libby's data is not usable for automation either way, so the recommendation does not change.

verdicts.claim: 7. Hardcover has a GraphQL API at api.hardcover.app/v1/graphql, Bearer token from settings, limits (60/min, 30s timeout, depth 3, 1000-row cap), user_book_reads fields and mutations.
verdicts.evidence: docs.hardcover.app returned HTTP 403 to fetch, and web search did not surface Hardcover's docs, so none of the endpoint or limit values were verified. The cited limits come from third-party GitHub issues. The claim's own note about a developer's header measurements already marks the daily figure as informal.
verdicts.correction: Treat limits as approximate and read the live rate-limit headers in the first call. Verify the endpoint, token page and mutation names via the GraphQL schema introspection or docs in a browser before building. The design needs only low polling volume (hourly, 2 users), so rate limits are not a risk.

verdicts.claim: 8. Apple Books exposes no progress/session data to Shortcuts or third parties; Screen Time per-app usage is not readable by a normal app; DeviceActivity/FamilyControls entitlement needs Apple approval.
verdicts.evidence: The fetch of https://developer.apple.com/documentation/deviceactivity returned only a title, and the summarizer answered from its own prior knowledge, so no primary-source text was verified. That knowledge is consistent with the claim: no raw numbers to the host app, opaque tokens, a sandboxed report extension, and a Family Controls entitlement that Apple must approve for distribution. Apple Books progress was not checked at all.
verdicts.correction: Keep the conclusion (Screen Time totals cannot be ingested into a backend; threshold events and an on-device report view are the only options) but mark it as unverified against Apple docs and re-check for iOS 26 changes. Note that the Family Controls distribution entitlement is requested through Apple, which may apply to TestFlight builds too; confirm before planning on it.

verification.revised_recommendation: Keep the layered structure, with these changes. (1) The manual timer and quick log stays as the guaranteed fallback. (2) Audiobookshelf stays the highest-automation audiobook path, but verify the session schema and the finished threshold on a live instance, and choose a client by testing offline sync and session reporting, since the third-party roster is larger and changing (ShelfPlayer, AudioBooth, SoundLeaf, Prologue, Audiary). The official iOS app is still a full early beta, so do not plan on it. (3) Hardcover is optional metadata only; verify the endpoint, mutations and limits yourself, since the docs were not reachable here. (4) Demote Audible and the audible-cli sidecar to a spike to validate against a real account, since the endpoint fields and aggregate windows are unverified and the project is mid-rewrite. Drop the 'low risk' wording on DRM removal. (5) Shortcuts automations stay unverified until tested on both phones. Screen Time ingestion should not be assumed possible: plan on threshold events or an on-device report only, and confirm the Family Controls entitlement path for TestFlight before committing to it. Overall confidence is lower than the researcher stated, because most claims could not be checked against primary sources in this pass.

findings.topic: Notifications, reminders, alarms and wake-up flows for a Flutter iOS app with a self-hosted Go/Node backend (no Firebase)

claims.claim: Server-side APNs with a .p8 key works in Go and Node. sideshow/apns2 README: token (JWT) auth via NewTokenClient with key, KeyID, TeamID; the key does not expire; supports interruptionLevel and relevanceScore; no mention of Live Activity push type. @parse/node-apn README: token auth with .p8 path, keyId, teamId; repo looks active (1,246 commits, CI badge). Neither README showed a last-release date.
claims.design_implication: Use Go sideshow/apns2 (or raw HTTP/2 + JWT) in the backend. One .p8 key serves dev and prod for both phones. If Live Activity pushes are wanted, check the lib sends apns-push-type liveactivity, else hand-roll that single call. Not verified: library release dates.

claims.claim: Flutter can receive APNs without Firebase via the 'push' package (v3.3.3, page says published ~21 months ago). Token via Push.instance.addOnNewToken; foreground via addOnMessage; background via addOnBackgroundMessage (top-level fn, separate isolate); launch tap via notificationTapWhichLaunchedAppFromTerminated and addOnNotificationTap. The page shows AppDelegate code only for macOS, none for iOS (so likely none needed on iOS - inferred). Force-quit apps get no background pushes. Page contradicts itself on simulator support. flutter_apns is discontinued and depends on firebase_messaging; flutter_apns_x is unmaintained.
claims.design_implication: Use 'push' just to obtain/refresh the device token and handle taps. Send visible aps.alert pushes so iOS renders them without Dart running. Package is stale; budget for a small native shim (about 30 lines in AppDelegate: registerForRemoteNotifications, forward didRegister token over a MethodChannel) as fallback.

claims.claim: Interruption levels (Apple page body did not load; table is from general knowledge, so verify): passive, active (default), timeSensitive (needs Time Sensitive Notifications capability/entitlement, user can disable per app, breaks Focus), critical (needs Apple-approved Critical Alerts entitlement, bypasses mute and Focus). flutter_local_notifications DarwinNotificationDetails verified to have an interruptionLevel field (iOS 15+), plus categoryIdentifier, threadIdentifier, criticalSoundVolume; enum values not seen.
claims.design_implication: Use timeSensitive for creatine/Huel/teeth reminders (just add the capability in Xcode, no Apple approval). Do not plan on critical; Apple approval is intended for health/safety and a personal TestFlight app is unlikely to qualify. For anything that must wake someone, use AlarmKit instead.

claims.claim: Notification actions: flutter_local_notifications (latest stable 22.3.3, needs Flutter 3.38.1+) supports iOS actions via DarwinNotificationCategory declared in initialize. The foreground option runs onDidReceiveNotificationResponse on the main isolate; without it the action runs in a background engine via onDidReceiveBackgroundNotificationResponse (top-level, @pragma vm:entry-point), with a documented warning that it may not wake the UI part of the app. Needs AppDelegate setPluginRegistrantCallback wiring, which differs under the UIScene lifecycle. Remote (server) pushes need a matching category registered at app start and aps.category in the payload; the category must be registered by flutter_local_notifications or native code.
claims.design_implication: Register categories like TAKE_SUPPLEMENT (Done/Snooze) and MEAL_LOG at startup. Make 'Done' background actions that POST to the backend directly (idempotent API), and have the server cancel the follow-up nag push. Test the background-action path on a real device, particularly with the app terminated.

claims.claim: AlarmKit (iOS 26): per WWDC25 session 230 text, alarms break through silent mode and Focus, show on Lock Screen, Dynamic Island, StandBy and paired Apple Watch. Requires NSAlarmKitUsageDescription and authorization (authorizationState notDetermined/authorized/denied; per-app opt-in). Schedules: fixed date, Relative(time, weekly repeats, tracks time zone changes), countdowns with preAlert/postAlert. Alert has a stop button and an optional secondary button whose behavior is .countdown (snooze) or .custom (runs a LiveActivityIntent passed as secondaryIntent, which can set openAppWhenRun = true to open the app with the alarm ID). Countdown alarms require a Live Activity widget extension. Custom sound must be in bundle or Library/Sounds. The page does not document any app callback at fire time. A GitHub PR report says a custom secondary intent leaves the alarm ringing until the app calls stop; unverified.
claims.design_implication: AlarmKit gives true wake-up alarms, but the system stop button can always dismiss it (Apple page text did not load; 'cannot prevent dismissal' is from general knowledge and the absence of any documented hook). A math-to-dismiss alarm is therefore NOT enforceable. Practical pattern: AlarmKit alarm with a custom secondary button 'Solve to earn points' that opens the app to a math screen; scoring rewards completion and the server checks whether the task was solved within N minutes, otherwise re-rings via a second alarm or a time-sensitive nag. Make it points-based, not blocking.

claims.claim: Flutter AlarmKit plugins exist. flutter_alarmkit 0.5.0 (publisher gdelataillade.me, ~10 days old on the fetch, 27 likes, 2.6k downloads, early/small): auth, one-shot/countdown/recurring alarms, getAlarms, alarmUpdates stream, pause/resume/restart/cancel/stop, custom sound (.caf/.aiff/.wav under 30 s), customizable Live Activity buttons/icons/colors, AlarmMetadata. Needs Flutter 3.38+, Xcode 26+, iOS 26 device; 'dart run flutter_alarmkit:setup' patches the iOS project and adds a WidgetKit extension in ios/AlarmkitWidget; calls on iOS below 26 throw UNSUPPORTED_VERSION. Its page does not mention custom button intents or open-app-on-tap. Also hinata-platform/alarm_kit exists (maximumLimitReached error; Apple does not publish the alarm limit). The widely used 'alarm' package does NOT use AlarmKit: it uses a silent AVAudioPlayer to keep the app awake, and when the app is killed only a warning notification is guaranteed on iOS.
claims.design_implication: Do not use the 'alarm' package on iOS. Start with flutter_alarmkit for schedule/cancel/stop, and expect to write a small custom Swift piece for the secondary-button LiveActivityIntent that deep-links to the math screen (verify the plugin's widget template exposes this; otherwise fork/edit the generated AlarmkitWidget and the intent). Since the alarm schedule is local, resync on every app open and via a silent push.

claims.claim: Live Activities need native code in any Flutter package. live_activities 2.6.0 (MIT, 660 likes, ~70k downloads, push-to-start iOS 17.2+, activityUpdateStream push tokens for server APNs updates) requires a Widget Extension in Xcode, App Groups, Push Notifications, NSSupportsLiveActivities, and SwiftUI written by hand. home_widget 0.10.0 handles home-screen widgets via shared storage: saveWidgetData then updateWidget(name:), with interactive widgets that call Dart; the widget UI must be native SwiftUI and its docs are at docs.page/abausg/home_widget (not fetched). live_activity_kit claims no-Swift Dart-defined UI, but it is unverified and obscure.
claims.design_implication: Streak/leaderboard widget: one WidgetKit extension in SwiftUI plus home_widget on the Dart side and a shared App Group. Live Activity (for example a workout timer or run) is optional and uses the same extension target. Put AlarmKit's widget, the home screen widget and any Live Activity in a single widget extension bundle to avoid maintaining several targets.

claims.claim: Scheduling reliability: iOS keeps only 64 pending local notifications (flutter_local_notifications docs: on iOS 10+ the 64 most recently set are kept). Background pushes (content-available, apns-push-type background, priority 5) are not guaranteed, are throttled, are not delivered to force-quit apps, may be deferred in Low Power Mode, and give about 30 s (the Apple doc body did not load; from general knowledge, verify). Apple guidance as recalled: use alert pushes for anything the user must see.
claims.design_implication: For fixed daily reminders (creatine, Huel, teeth AM/PM), local repeating notifications are the most reliable (work offline, use 1 pending slot each with a repeating calendar trigger). Use server visible pushes for dynamic, state-dependent messages (streak about to break, partner overtook you, no dinner logged, adaptive nag-until-done) because the server knows completion state and can skip or cancel. Do not rely on background fetch or silent pushes to reschedule things.

findings.recommended_approach: Hybrid, three tiers. (1) Local repeating notifications via flutter_local_notifications for the fixed daily habits (creatine/Huel, teeth AM/PM, bedtime wind-down), with interruptionLevel timeSensitive, an actions category (Done/Snooze) whose background handler POSTs to the backend. Keep well under 64 pending; use repeating calendar triggers, not unrolled schedules. (2) Server-driven visible APNs pushes (Go + sideshow/apns2, one .p8 key, device token from the 'push' package registered per user at /devices) for state-dependent nudges: streak-at-risk, partner overtakes, no dinner logged by 5pm, weekly recap; set aps.category for actions and interruption-level appropriately (active for most, timeSensitive sparingly, passive for recaps); the server cancels or skips the nag when completion is already recorded. Use content-available pushes only as best-effort hints to resync state. (3) AlarmKit for the morning wake-up alarm only (flutter_alarmkit), with a custom secondary button that opens a math/wake-check screen; scoring and a server-side check reward solving it, because a hard 'cannot dismiss until solved' is not possible. Home screen streak widget through home_widget + one SwiftUI WidgetKit extension in a shared App Group; Live Activities optional later via live_activities package using the same extension.\n\nNative pieces that cannot be pure Dart: (a) Xcode capabilities: Push Notifications, Background Modes -> Remote notifications, Time Sensitive Notifications, App Groups; Info.plist NSAlarmKitUsageDescription (and NSSupportsLiveActivities if used); (b) WidgetKit extension target in SwiftUI (home screen streak widget, AlarmKit alarm/countdown Live Activity UI, optional workout Live Activity), generated mainly by 'dart run flutter_alarmkit:setup'; (c) a Swift LiveActivityIntent for the AlarmKit secondary button (openAppWhenRun, alarm ID passed, deep link to the math screen) and likely a stop call from the intent; (d) AppDelegate wiring for flutter_local_notifications background actions (setPluginRegistrantCallback, different under UIScene lifecycle); (e) possibly a tiny APNs token shim if the stale 'push' package misbehaves on iOS 26; (f) the Apple Developer portal APNs key (.p8) and TestFlight build with aps-environment entitlement. Everything else (scheduling logic, API calls, UI, math puzzle, token registration) is Dart.
alternatives: Skip 'push' and use a tiny native Swift shim plus MethodChannel for APNs token and tap handling: less dependence on a 21-month-old package, about 30-50 lines of Swift.
All reminders via server pushes only: simpler single source of truth, but they fail when the phone is offline or the home server is down; fixed daily habits are better done locally.

Skip AlarmKit and use time-sensitive notification chains (for example repeated notifications every minute) as a wake-up: works on all iOS versions but cannot ring through the mute switch and is poor UX; the 'alarm' package keeps a silent audio session alive and is unreliable once the app is killed.
Use Shortcuts/Clock alarm: the user sets a normal Clock alarm and the app only handles the post-wake check-in (open app, solve math, log weight); no native alarm code at all.
Use live_activity_kit (claims no Swift) to avoid writing SwiftUI, but unverified and obscure; not recommended for a long-lived app.
cannot_do: Force an AlarmKit alarm to remain ringing until a math problem is solved: the stop button always works, and no documented hook lets the app block dismissal (the Apple doc body did not load, so this rests on the absence of any such API plus general knowledge; verify).
Run Dart or app code at the moment an AlarmKit alarm fires; the only documented hook is the secondary-button intent triggered by the user.
Use Critical Alerts without Apple's approved entitlement; not realistic for this app.
Guarantee delivery of silent/background pushes or background fetch for reminders, especially when the app was force-quit or Low Power Mode is on.
Schedule more than 64 pending local notifications (iOS silently keeps only 64).
Use AlarmKit on devices below iOS 26 (plugins throw UNSUPPORTED_VERSION); fine here since both phones can run iOS 26, but Apple Watch alarm behavior is unverified.
Write the widget or Live Activity UI in Dart; it must be SwiftUI in a WidgetKit extension.
open_questions_for_user: Is a math-to-dismiss alarm a hard requirement, or is 'alarm rings, then app prompts a math check-in that earns points' acceptable, given the system stop button cannot be blocked?
Are both phones definitely on iOS 26 (needed for AlarmKit)?
Do you want a Live Activity (for example a workout or run timer in the Dynamic Island) in v1, or just a home screen streak widget?
Are you comfortable owning a small amount of Swift (widget extension, AlarmKit intent, AppDelegate wiring) alongside Flutter?
Should reminders keep working when your home server is down? If yes, keep the daily habit reminders fully local.

verdicts.claim: 1. APNs .p8 server-side works in Go (sideshow/apns2) and Node (@parse/node-apn); both maintained
verdicts.evidence: Token auth is confirmed. Verified now: node-apn latest release 8.1.0 on 2026-04-12, which added push type 'widgets' (#194), so it is actively maintained (https://github.com/parse-community/node-apn/releases). sideshow/apns2 has 192 commits, no GitHub releases, and its latest master commit I could see was 2025-07-22, 'Upgrade to Go 1.18 and update dependencies' (https://github.com/sideshow/apns2/commits/master). Low activity, not dead. The README has no mention of a liveactivity push type.
verdicts.correction: node-apn is actively maintained (8.1.0, Apr 2026). apns2 works but has been quiet since mid-2025. Check that its PushType field accepts 'liveactivity' and 'alarm' before relying on it for Live Activity pushes. Otherwise a raw HTTP/2 + JWT client in Go is about 100 lines and removes the dependency risk.

verdicts.claim: 2. Flutter can receive APNs without Firebase via the 'push' package 3.3.3; no iOS AppDelegate code needed
verdicts.evidence: Verified: version 3.3.3, published 21 months ago, verified publisher orth.uk. The iOS section has no AppDelegate requirement. Only macOS needs the three forwarding methods. The simulator notes contradict each other (https://pub.dev/packages/push). The package has not been released since roughly early 2025, so it predates iOS 26/27 and the Flutter UIScene migration. Flutter 3.41 makes UIScene the default and the iOS 27 SDK requires it. Whether push's token and delegate hooks work under UIScene is unverified.
verdicts.correction: The package exists and its docs say no iOS AppDelegate change is needed. It is stale, though, and not tested against UIScene. Keep the 'tiny native shim' fallback in the plan. The shim is a few lines in AppDelegate that calls registerForRemoteNotifications and forwards the token over a MethodChannel. Test on a real device early.

verdicts.claim: 3. Interruption levels (passive, active, timeSensitive needs capability, critical needs Apple entitlement); flutter_local_notifications has interruptionLevel
verdicts.evidence: The Apple page body would not load, so I could not verify it against the primary source. Secondary summary matches the claim: passive, active (default), timeSensitive (Time Sensitive Notifications capability), critical (special Apple entitlement, bypasses mute and DND). Apple's own docs are consistent with this from memory. The interruptionLevel field in DarwinNotificationDetails was not re-fetched.
verdicts.correction: Treat as likely true, unverified against Apple. A correction: iOS 26 did not change these rules as far as I found. Two users makes critical alerts moot, since Apple approval is not realistic for a TestFlight app.

verdicts.claim: 4. flutter_local_notifications 22.3.3, Flutter 3.38.1+, DarwinNotificationCategory actions, foreground vs background handler, AppDelegate registrant wiring differs under UIScene
verdicts.evidence: https://pub.dev/packages/flutter_local_notifications shows 22.3.3 (published 43 hours before capture), SDK Flutter 3.38.1, prerelease 23.0.0-dev.5. Background handler runs in a separate engine, must be top-level with @pragma('vm:entry-point'), and the iOS plugin registrant callback must be registered in AppDelegate. Actions with the foreground option run on the main isolate. Under UIScene, move the registrant callback to didInitializeImplicitFlutterEngine; otherwise it stays in didFinishLaunchingWithOptions. The UNUserNotificationCenterDelegate should still be set in didFinishLaunchingWithOptions (changelog 21.0.0). The 64-pending limit is confirmed: on iOS 10+ the 64 most recently scheduled are kept.
verdicts.correction: Add: the iOS 27 SDK requires UIScene, so the UIScene wiring path is the one to plan for. Flutter 3.41+ auto-migrates only an unmodified AppDelegate, and this app will have a customized one. Note the 64 limit applies to the 64 most recently scheduled, not the soonest, on iOS 10+. The doc-based claim about 'may not wake UI' and the remote-push category requirement were not independently re-verified.

verdicts.claim: 5. AlarmKit (iOS 26) behavior: breaks silent/Focus, NSAlarmKitUsageDescription, authorization, schedules, stop plus secondary button (.countdown/.custom with LiveActivityIntent, openAppWhenRun), countdown needs Live Activity extension
verdicts.evidence: Apple's docs page body did not load (title only), so the claim rests on the WWDC transcript the researcher read (https://developer.apple.com/videos/play/wwdc2025/230/). New findings: (a) a Medium post says openAppWhenRun is deprecated in iOS 26.0 in favor of supportedModes, with .foreground(.immediate) equivalent (https://toyboy2.medium.com/migrating-from-usernotifications-to-alarmkit-in-ios-26-3ed81a53a7b7), unconfirmed against Apple; (b) the same source says iOS 26.1 changed the stop control to a slider; (c) the iOS 27 SDK adds new AlarmManager.AlarmConfiguration factories (countdown, timer(duration:), alarm(schedule:)) with optional stop intent and secondary intent, and deprecates nothing (https://miniswift.run/whats-new/alarmkit/). Forum and GitHub threads show custom secondary button issues with no resolution found.
verdicts.correction: Core claims are plausible. Revise: use supportedModes instead of openAppWhenRun (the older property may be deprecated). Add a stop intent, which the iOS 27 SDK makes first-class. Whether a custom secondary intent leaves the alarm ringing is still unresolved; call stop explicitly in the intent's perform and test on a device on 26.1+.

verdicts.claim: 6. Flutter AlarmKit plugins: flutter_alarmkit 0.5.0 (about 10 days old) and others; 'alarm' package does not use AlarmKit
verdicts.evidence: https://pub.dev/packages/flutter_alarmkit: 0.5.0, published 10 days ago, needs Flutter 3.38.0+, Xcode 26+, iOS 26+, throws UNSUPPORTED_VERSION on older iOS, supports SPM and CocoaPods. Features match the claim. The page does not describe custom button intents or open-app. NEW in 0.5.0 changelog: the App Group requirement is dropped (issue #21), setup ships a new widget template, and the entitlement group.flutter-alarmkit is removed. Re-run 'dart run flutter_alarmkit:setup' after upgrading and use --doctor. The hinata-platform/alarm_kit and 'alarm' package details were not re-fetched.
verdicts.correction: Remove 'needs App Group' for flutter_alarmkit; 0.5.0 no longer needs it (home_widget and live_activities still do, so you may add one anyway). The plugin lacks a custom secondary intent. For the math-screen flow that means writing your own Swift AlarmConfiguration and intent, or forking the plugin. This is a bigger native footprint than the recommendation implies.

verdicts.claim: 7. Live Activities need native code; live_activities 2.6.0 (660 likes, ~70k downloads, push-to-start iOS 17.2+); home_widget 0.10.0
verdicts.evidence: https://pub.dev/packages/live_activities confirms 2.6.0, 660 likes, 150 pub points, 70.3k downloads, published 45 days ago. It needs a Widget Extension, Push Notifications on Runner, App Groups on both targets, NSSupportsLiveActivities in both Info.plists, and a LiveActivitiesAppAttributes struct with that exact name. Minimum is iOS 16.1. It supports push-to-start tokens (iOS 17.2+), although the author advises against that approach. The license, the home_widget 0.10.0 details and the live_activity_kit claim were not re-fetched.
verdicts.correction: Confirmed for live_activities. Add that the extension needs the exact struct name LiveActivitiesAppAttributes. home_widget and live_activity_kit claims remain unverified. A shared widget extension for the alarm, home widget and Live Activity will conflict with the names and App Group the plugins each generate. Expect manual merging.

verdicts.claim: 8. Scheduling reliability: 64 pending local notifications; background pushes unreliable, throttled, not delivered when force-quit, about 30 s
verdicts.evidence: The 64 limit is verified in the flutter_local_notifications docs (https://pub.dev/packages/flutter_local_notifications). The Apple background-updates doc did not load, so the throttling, force-quit and 30 s claims are from general knowledge and the push package page ('force-quit apps will not handle push notifications' with a contradictory note that they 'can receive push notifications now').
verdicts.correction: Keep the 64 claim. Treat the background-push claims as likely true and unverified against Apple. Design so correctness never depends on background pushes: always sync on app open.

verification.revised_recommendation: The three-tier structure stands, with these changes. (1) Re-baseline the platform. The search results say the iOS 27 SDK exists and requires UIScene (apps built with it won't launch otherwise), and Flutter 3.41+ makes UIScene the default and auto-migrates only an unmodified AppDelegate. The brief says iOS 26 / Xcode 26 is current, which looks outdated, so confirm that and plan on UIScene from the start. Put the flutter_local_notifications registrant callback in didInitializeImplicitFlutterEngine and keep the UNUserNotificationCenter delegate in didFinishLaunchingWithOptions. (2) Treat the 'push' package (3.3.3, last released about 21 months ago) as a risk. Prototype token registration on a real device early, and keep a small native AppDelegate shim ready that forwards the device token over a MethodChannel. (3) On the server, node-apn is verifiably active (8.1.0, April 2026), but apns2 has had little activity since July 2025. If staying in Go, consider a thin HTTP/2 + JWT client of your own so alert, background, liveactivity and alarm push types are fully controlled. (4) AlarmKit: flutter_alarmkit 0.5.0 covers scheduling, but not a custom secondary-button intent or open-app. Expect to write that part in Swift or fork the plugin.
