Use supportedModes (openAppWhenRun is reportedly deprecated), add an explicit stop intent, call stop in the intent, and test on iOS 26.1+. App Groups are no longer required by flutter_alarmkit 0.5.0. Home widget and Live Activities still need one. Verify against Apple's own docs for the unverified items: interruption levels, AlarmKit, and background push limits.

findings.topic: Private Flutter iOS distribution to two iPhones for a year without App Store review

claims.claim: TestFlight builds expire 90 days after upload and become unavailable to testers. Limits: 100 internal testers (App Store Connect users with access), 10,000 external.
claims.design_implication: Upload a fresh build at least every 60 days (ideally on a schedule). An expiry disables the app on both phones at once. Add an in-app build-age warning.

claims.claim: External testing sends the first build of a group to Beta App Review. Apple's overview page does not say internal testing needs review; secondary sources say internal builds skip Beta App Review and are available within minutes of processing. Internal testers must be members of the App Store Connect team, so Nadia needs an App Store Connect user invite with her Apple ID.
claims.design_implication: Use an internal group only and never create an external group. The Apple internal-tester help page returned 404, so the exact role names are from general knowledge; verify in the App Store Connect UI. Set ITSAppUsesNonExemptEncryption=false in Info.plist to skip the export-compliance prompt on each upload (inferred, standard practice).

claims.claim: Since 2026-04-28 all App Store Connect uploads (TestFlight included) must be built with Xcode 26+ against the iOS 26 SDK. The deployment target is independent of the SDK.
claims.design_implication: CI images must have Xcode 26. Pin the Xcode version in CI and expect a similar yearly SDK bump each spring, which is a recurring maintenance item.

claims.claim: Ad hoc and development profiles allow up to 100 registered devices per product family per membership year. Disabling a device does not free a slot; the list can be reset only at the membership renewal. Ad hoc builds expire with their provisioning profile (at most 1 year, third-party sources). TestFlight does not use this device quota.
claims.design_implication: Ad hoc is a workable fallback with 2 iPhones (2 Watches count as a separate family) but it needs UDID registration and a re-sign at least yearly, and it does not give push-friendly update tooling. Keep it as a backup, not the primary path.

claims.claim: Xcode direct install with a paid account uses a development profile, believed to last about 1 year (not verified on an Apple page). A free Apple ID gets 7-day profiles (general knowledge, not verified here). Nadia's phone would need to be connected to Nick's Mac for each reinstall.
claims.design_implication: Good for dev iteration on Nick's own phone, bad for Nadia's. Do not rely on it for her. Also, HealthKit background delivery and some capabilities work the same under dev signing, so it is a useful debugging path.

claims.claim: Apple Developer Enterprise Program is not applicable (requires 100+ employees, org eligibility). AltStore and other sideloading are not needed. These are general knowledge claims, not verified from a fetched source in this run. In the EU, alternative marketplaces exist but the user is presumably US-based (not asked).
claims.design_implication: Rule these out; TestFlight internal covers the need with less operational risk.

claims.claim: Xcode Cloud: every Apple Developer Program membership includes 25 compute hours per month at no extra cost (since Jan 2024). Flutter's official docs give an ios/ci_scripts/ci_post_clone.sh that clones Flutter stable, runs flutter precache --ios, flutter pub get, installs CocoaPods and pod install. The script must be committed executable, and must live under ios/ci_scripts. Xcode Cloud needs the workflow created from Xcode on a Mac once.
claims.design_implication: Xcode Cloud is the zero-cost, zero-secret route (signing and TestFlight upload are managed by Apple), but the first-time workflow creation requires Xcode on a Mac (a borrowed Mac or a cloud Mac rental for one session). A Linux-only dev cannot create the workflow. Pin the Flutter version in the script rather than tracking stable HEAD (inference) for reproducibility.

claims.claim: Codemagic: personal accounts get 500 free macOS M2 build minutes per month, 1 concurrent build, no free minutes on Linux or for teams; overage about $0.095/min. Codemagic can sign automatically via an App Store Connect API key and publish to TestFlight with no Mac on the developer side.
claims.design_implication: Best no-Mac option: one Flutter iOS build takes roughly 10-20 min (inference), so 500 min/month covers about 25-50 builds, far more than needed. Verify the live pricing page before committing.

claims.claim: GitHub Actions macOS runners bill at 10x the Linux minute rate; public repos with standard runners are free; private repos on the Free plan have a monthly quota (commonly 2,000 minutes, about 200 macOS minutes; figure from a secondary source, not confirmed in GitHub text). Default spending limit of $0 blocks overage.
claims.design_implication: A public repo gives free macOS builds, but this repo holds personal health logic and secrets handling so private is likelier; then 200 macOS minutes is about 10-15 builds/month, still enough for a release cadence of a few per month. Keep secrets only in GitHub Secrets if public (inference).

claims.claim: fastlane flow (Flutter docs): flutter build ipa, then build_app(skip_build_archive: true, archive_path: ...) and upload_to_testflight; use fastlane match to sync distribution certs on ephemeral CI, pin fastlane via Gemfile, run flutter build ios --release --no-codesign --config-only first. App Store Connect API key (Key ID, Issuer ID, .p8 shown once) replaces password/2FA; this part is general knowledge, not from the fetched page.
claims.design_implication: Use an ASC API key (never an Apple ID password) in CI. match needs a private git repo (can be Nick's own self-hosted Gitea or a private GitHub repo) to store the encrypted certs and requires the Admin role for the key to create certs. Alternative: Codemagic or Xcode managed signing avoids match.

claims.claim: Flutter 3.35 raised the minimum iOS deployment target from 12 to 13 (auto-migrated). The `health` package (13.3.0 seen) wraps HealthKit on iOS; setup needs the HealthKit capability in Xcode and NSHealthShareUsageDescription (and NSHealthUpdateUsageDescription if writing) in Info.plist. Enabling HealthKit adds it to required device capabilities (UIRequiredDeviceCapabilities), which is fine for iPhones.
claims.design_implication: Target iOS 17 or 18 minimum in practice (both phones are current; inference) to use modern Swift/SwiftUI-bridge APIs, and set it explicitly in Xcode and the Podfile. The pub.dev health 13.3.0 page was only seen via search snippets; confirm the package's own iOS minimum and its background-delivery support when picking it.

claims.claim: Background Modes, App Groups and push capability setup in Xcode: not verified from a source in this run. From general knowledge: add capabilities under Signing & Capabilities (HealthKit incl. 'Background Delivery', Background Modes: background fetch/remote notifications, App Groups for Watch app or widget sharing, Push Notifications), these update the explicit App ID in the developer portal and are baked into the provisioning profile, so any capability change requires a re-signed build. Push requires an APNs auth key (.p8) via developer portal. HealthKit background delivery requires the HKObserverQuery plus enableBackgroundDelivery, which the Flutter `health` package may not expose, so a small native Swift plugin is likely needed.
claims.design_implication: Decide capabilities up front before the first TestFlight upload. Plan a small Swift method-channel plugin for HealthKit observer queries and watchOS companion pieces. Do the capability setup once on a Mac (or in Codemagic with automatic signing, which creates the App ID capabilities via the API). Verify each against Apple docs when implementing.

claims.claim: Shorebird code push: usable on iOS (custom Dart interpreter for patched code) and vendor says it complies with App Store rules if the patch does not change the app's primary purpose. Only Dart changes can be patched (native or new native plugins require a new release), patches only run in Release builds on physical arm64 devices, and only Flutter's stable channel is supported. The FAQ says it cannot gate patches to TestFlight groups, so patches reach any install of that release; workaround is flavors/separate bundle IDs. Free tier: sources say about 5,000 patch installs/month, which is ample for 2 users; paid price figures conflict ($20/month vs $240/year) so check the live page. TestFlight compatibility is not explicitly documented.
claims.design_implication: Shorebird is optional. It saves rebuild minutes and the 90-day treadmill only partly, since the base binary still expires at 90 days in TestFlight, so a re-upload is mandatory regardless. Since the only users are two people in internal testing and Apple's TestFlight is a beta channel, ship patches there at low policy risk (inference, not Apple-confirmed). A cheaper alternative is to make most behavior server-driven (workout plans, scoring rules, copy) from the Go/Next backend so fewer client changes are needed.

findings.recommended_approach: PRIMARY: TestFlight internal testing only (no Beta App Review, no device UDIDs, no profile registration quota). Steps: (1) Add Nadia as an App Store Connect user with a role allowed for internal testing and create one internal group. (2) CI without a Mac: Codemagic personal free tier (500 macOS M2 min/month) with an App Store Connect API key, automatic signing and publishing to TestFlight; trigger on a git tag and on a monthly scheduled build so a build is never older than ~60 days. Backup CI if Nick prefers a self-contained repo: GitHub Actions macOS runner with fastlane match + pilot (200 macOS minutes on a private Free plan, unlimited on a public repo), or Xcode Cloud (25 free hours/month, no secrets, but first workflow setup needs Xcode on a Mac once). If Nick has a Mac: do local Xcode install for fast iteration on his phone via a development profile, use flutter build ipa + fastlane upload_to_testflight, or Xcode Cloud. (3) Keep Dart-only fixes cheap with either (a) server-driven content/config from the self-hosted backend, plus (b) optional Shorebird free tier patches on the TestFlight release (note it cannot target a TestFlight group and the base build still expires in 90 days). (4) Set capabilities (HealthKit, Background Modes, App Groups, Push) once before the first upload since they live in the App ID and provisioning profile. FALLBACK: ad hoc with both iPhones' UDIDs (valid for the profile lifetime, up to 1 year) if TestFlight misbehaves. MAINTENANCE CALENDAR: weekly/automatic none; every ~30 days: scheduled CI build uploaded (keeps newest build <60 days; the hard limit is 90 days); each TestFlight build: accept/update in the TestFlight app and check that the app launches; every spring (Apple raises the minimum SDK, e.g. the 2026-04-28 Xcode 26 rule): bump Xcode/Flutter version in CI; every September to October after new iOS ships: update Xcode, Flutter and plugins and retest HealthKit; every year at membership renewal: renew the $99 Apple Developer Program (lapse stops uploads and eventually removes TestFlight), renew/reissue the distribution certificate (valid 1 year) and refresh provisioning profiles (1 year) via match nuke or Codemagic regen, accept updated Apple agreements in App Store Connect, review/rotate the App Store Connect API key (no expiry, but revocable) and the APNs key (no expiry); if using ad hoc, re-register devices and reset device list at renewal; on any capability change: rebuild and re-sign.
alternatives: Ad hoc distribution via Codemagic/fastlane or Diawi-style install page: 100-device/year quota, profile up to 1 year, no 90-day cliff but needs UDID registration and a yearly re-sign. Good backup.
Xcode direct install from a Mac with a paid account: about 1-year dev profile (unverified), requires physical connection for Nadia's phone, so only Nick's phone is practical.
Xcode Cloud only: zero secrets and 25 free hours/month, but requires a Mac once to create the workflow.
GitHub Actions + fastlane match: most controllable and keeps everything in the repo; macOS minutes are 10x and limited on private Free plans.
Self-hosted Mac mini runner or a rented Mac (MacStadium, AWS EC2 Mac has a 24h minimum): overkill for a 2-user app.
AltStore/SideStore: free-account style 7-day re-signing, unnecessary with a paid account.
Apple Developer Enterprise Program: not eligible for a 2-person private use.
cannot_do: Could not verify from Apple's own pages that internal TestFlight skips Beta App Review (Apple's overview only mentions review for external testers); the claim rests on secondary sources.
Apple's internal-tester help URL returned 404, so exact roles for internal testers are unconfirmed.
Could not confirm the GitHub Free plan's 2,000-minute private-repo allowance from an official page.
Did not verify the dev-profile 1-year validity, certificate lifetimes, 7-day free-profile limit, Shorebird's current paid price, or Shorebird behavior inside TestFlight on an official source.
Did not verify HealthKit/Background Modes/App Groups/Push Xcode setup details or the `health` package's background-delivery support from primary documentation.
Did not research watchOS companion app packaging in Flutter.
open_questions_for_user: Does Nick own or have access to a Mac (even occasionally)? That decides Xcode Cloud vs Codemagic as the primary CI.
Is the Apple Developer account individual or organization, and is Nick the Account Holder (needed to add Nadia as an App Store Connect user and create API keys)?
Will the app need a watchOS companion app (on-wrist workout logging) or is HealthKit read-only from the iPhone enough? A watch app changes signing, capabilities and the build.
Is the repo public or private on GitHub (affects free macOS minutes)?
Comfortable with the app depending on a monthly CI re-upload, or prefer ad hoc as the primary to avoid the 90-day cliff?
Which Flutter HealthKit approach: the `health` package, or a custom Swift plugin for background delivery?

verdicts.claim: 1. TestFlight builds expire after 90 days; 100 internal testers, 10,000 external
verdicts.evidence: Apple TestFlight overview (https://developer.apple.com/help/app-store-connect/test-a-beta-version/testflight-overview): 90 days, up to 100 App Store Connect users, up to 10,000 external testers.
verdicts.correction: None.

verdicts.claim: 2. Internal testing skips Beta App Review; internal testers must be App Store Connect users, so Nadia needs an invite
verdicts.evidence: Apple page (same URL) says the first build added to an external group goes to review and that review is 'required only for the first build'. It never states internal builds are exempt and implies they are not reviewed. The 'must be an App Store Connect user' part follows from the '100 App Store Connect users' wording.
verdicts.correction: Internal exemption is implied by Apple's page, not stated, and the 'available within minutes' timing is from secondary sources only. Treat it as likely true. Verify on the first upload.

verdicts.claim: 3. Since 2026-04-28 uploads need Xcode 26+ and the iOS 26 SDK; deployment target is independent
verdicts.evidence: https://developer.apple.com/news/upcoming-requirements/ says apps uploaded to App Store Connect from April 28, 2026 must be built with Xcode 26 or later using the iOS 26 (and sibling) SDK. The deployment-target independence is general knowledge and was not checked on the page.
verdicts.correction: None. Mark the deployment-target sentence as inferred.

verdicts.claim: 4. Ad hoc/development: 100 devices per product family per membership year; disabling doesn't free a slot; reset only at renewal; TestFlight doesn't use the quota
verdicts.evidence: https://developer.apple.com/help/account/devices/devices-overview: 100 per product family per membership year; disabling does not increase the count; at renewal Account Holder/Admin/App Manager can remove devices to restore the count. The 1-year profile lifetime and TestFlight not using the quota were not checked on Apple pages.
verdicts.correction: Add that devices can be removed at renewal, not that the list is reset automatically. The page also says a device list can be downloaded 30 days before expiry, and devices are removed 180 days after membership expiry.

verdicts.claim: 5. Xcode Cloud: 25 free compute hours/month; Flutter's ci_post_clone.sh; executable and under ios/ci_scripts; workflow created once from Xcode on a Mac
verdicts.evidence: https://developer.apple.com/xcode-cloud/ lists 25 compute hours/month included with membership. https://docs.flutter.dev/deployment/cd shows ios/ci_scripts/ci_post_clone.sh with git clone of flutter stable, flutter precache --ios, flutter pub get, brew install cocoapods, pod install, plus 'git add --chmod=+x'. The page says to configure the workflow in Xcode; Apple says 'Configure a workflow in Xcode'.
verdicts.correction: Minor: the Flutter script installs CocoaPods via Homebrew. The 'since Jan 2024' detail was not re-checked. The page says the workflow is configured in Xcode, so a Mac is needed for the first setup, though App Store Connect's web dashboard can edit workflows afterward.

verdicts.claim: 6. Codemagic personal: 500 free macOS M2 min/month, 1 concurrent build, no free Linux or team minutes, overage ~$0.095/min; API-key signing and TestFlight publishing with no Mac
verdicts.evidence: https://codemagic.io/pricing and https://docs.codemagic.io/billing/pricing/: 500 free macOS M2 minutes/month for personal accounts, 1 concurrency, no free minutes for Teams, no free Linux, M2 $0.095/min (M4 $0.114), overage billed only if billing is enabled. API-key signing was not re-fetched. It is a documented Codemagic feature.
verdicts.correction: Add that a personal plan cannot invite collaborators, and that M4 costs more at $0.114/min. Nick must verify the free tier still applies when he signs up.

verdicts.claim: 7. GitHub Actions macOS is 10x Linux; public repos free; Free plan 2,000 min (~200 macOS min); default $0 spending limit blocks overage
verdicts.evidence: https://docs.github.com/en/billing/concepts/product-billing/github-actions: Free plan has 2,000 minutes/month with no macOS breakdown; macOS 3-/4-core is $0.062/min vs Linux 2-core $0.006/min (about 10.3x); standard runners are free in public repos. The page does not state the default spending limit.
verdicts.correction: Rate ratio is about 10x and the 2,000 figure is confirmed, but the 200 macOS minutes figure is an inference from the 10x ratio. The $0 default limit is not confirmed on this page. Note that a payment method on file means spending is governed by budgets.

verdicts.claim: 8. fastlane flow from Flutter docs: flutter build ipa, build_app(skip_build_archive...), upload_to_testflight; match; Gemfile; --no-codesign --config-only; ASC API key replaces password/2FA
verdicts.evidence: https://docs.flutter.dev/deployment/cd shows the build_app/upload_to_testflight lane, match, Gemfile with bundle exec, and 'flutter build ios --release --no-codesign --config-only'. The docs only mention FASTLANE_PASSWORD (iTunes Connect password) and say nothing about API keys.
verdicts.correction: The API key point is general fastlane knowledge, which the researcher already flagged. Flutter's doc still describes password-based auth, which triggers 2FA on CI. Recommend the API key for CI. Also note that the doc's cited 'Keep credentials out of the server' phrase and the lane need `flutter build ipa` run first, as the claim says.

verification.revised_recommendation: The recommendation stands. TestFlight internal testing is still the primary path, with the same Codemagic personal free tier, Xcode Cloud and GitHub Actions backups, and an ad hoc fallback. Four edits are needed. (1) Mark the internal-testing exemption from Beta App Review as likely but unverified, and check it on the first upload. (2) Drop the specific '200 macOS minutes' and '$0 default limit' figures for GitHub Actions. Say instead that the Free plan has 2,000 minutes and macOS bills at about 10x. (3) Note that a Codemagic personal plan cannot have collaborators. (4) In the ad hoc fallback and maintenance calendar, say that device slots are freed by removing devices at renewal, not by an automatic reset. I did not verify the 90-day schedule advice, Shorebird behavior, certificate and profile lifetimes, or APNs key expiry, so keep them marked as unverified. The monthly rebuild cadence is sound because the 90-day expiry is confirmed.

findings.topic: Blood-test ingestion, supplement nudges, supplement adherence, and toothbrushing tracking

claims.claim: Lab results from Apple Health Records are stored as read-only HKClinicalRecord samples (type HKClinicalType.labResultsRecord) whose fhirResource property holds the raw FHIR Observation JSON, normally with LOINC codes. Third-party apps can read them with per-type user permission.
claims.design_implication: A native Swift HealthKit bridge can pull labs as FHIR JSON and upload it to the Go backend. The backend maps by LOINC, not by printed test name.

claims.claim: Reading clinical records needs the HealthKit capability with Clinical Health Records enabled, plus the Info.plist keys NSHealthShareUsageDescription and NSHealthClinicalHealthRecordsShareUsageDescription. A paid team can use it in development builds. One personal project reports Apple reviews the entitlement only at App Review and that a free team cannot use it. I did not verify whether it works through TestFlight, which has a lighter beta review. Verify this early with a spike.
claims.design_implication: Do a day-one spike on a real TestFlight build before relying on the HealthKit clinical path. Keep PDF upload as the guaranteed fallback.

claims.claim: Apple Health Records only has data if a provider is connected in Health. Labcorp (account-based, 2018) and Quest (MyQuest account) joined the program, and many Epic-based health systems also feed it. I found no current Apple page listing supported institutions, so current status is unverified. One Epic (Kaiser) export came as multi-coded Observations (several LOINC codings per record), and effective dates had to be taken from FHIR effectiveDateTime because the HealthKit start date is the ingestion time.
claims.design_implication: Ask Nick and Nadia which lab or health system they use. Parse every coding on each Observation and use effectiveDateTime as the test date.

claims.claim: Shortcuts cannot read clinical records, and most lab analytes (A1c, lipids, ferritin etc.) have no standard HealthKit quantity type. Only a few such as glucose map. The manual alternative is the Health app's Export All Health Data zip, which includes the FHIR JSON.
claims.design_implication: Do not rely on Shortcuts for labs. Store labs in your own Postgres table (loinc, value, unit, ref_low, ref_high, flag, date) rather than writing them back to HealthKit.

claims.claim: For PDFs, existing projects use LLM vision/OCR or deterministic parsers. Vendors (Volo Health, Sensible) pipeline extraction, LOINC mapping and UCUM unit normalization. Quest and Labcorp layouts differ, and some panel rows have no clean LOINC match. In one hand-audit (LabLedger, 88 rows from 5 reports), 4 rows were wrong, including a misread positive result taken from the reference column. No peer-reviewed accuracy benchmark was found.
claims.design_implication: Use a vision LLM to extract rows into a strict JSON schema, with the reference range and flag read from the same row. Then show a mandatory human review table (value, unit, range, date) beside the PDF page before saving. Validate with plausibility bounds and a unit check, and send unmatched LOINC rows to manual selection.

claims.claim: Safe supplement mappings (from my background knowledge, not verified this session because NIH ODS pages returned 403): low 25(OH)D -> vitamin D3 at moderate dose with retest in about 8-12 weeks and an upper intake of 4000 IU/day for adults; low B12 -> oral B12 with a note to see a clinician about cause (pernicious anemia, metformin, etc.); low ferritin -> diet first and discuss with a clinician before iron; magnesium supplements are capped at 350 mg/day from supplements (UL) and serum magnesium is a poor marker of body stores. Iron is the riskiest because men and non-deficient people can overload (hemochromatosis).
claims.design_implication: Ship a small hand-curated rules table (marker, condition, suggestion, max dose, retest interval, doctor-flag). Verify each row against NIH ODS in a browser before coding. Never auto-recommend iron or high-dose anything, and never let an LLM generate dosages.

claims.claim: Creatine: the ISSN 2017 position reports no compelling evidence of renal harm in healthy people, and serum creatinine rises as a predictable effect of larger creatine pools rather than nephrotoxicity. Evidence for people with existing kidney disease is limited. Secondary sources only; the primary paper was not retrieved.
claims.design_implication: When creatinine or eGFR is outside range for a user taking creatine, show an informational note that creatine can raise creatinine, so ask the clinician. Do not label it kidney damage. Include a creatine tag on the lab-review screen.

claims.claim: HealthKit has no dietary supplement type for creatine or Huel. Nutrition types (dietary energy, protein etc.) exist, and Huel could be logged as nutrition. Creatine has no calories to speak of. Supplement adherence is therefore app-owned data.
claims.design_implication: Store adherence in your own Postgres table (user, item, taken_at, source). Optionally write Huel as dietary energy and protein to HealthKit through the food-log path.

claims.claim: NFC tag Shortcuts personal automations can run with 'Ask Before Running' off, triggering a Shortcut in the background. Sources disagree about whether the phone must be unlocked. Some actions still prompt. Apps cannot read an NFC tag and act silently on their own, so the workaround is the tag firing a Shortcut that calls the app or an HTTP endpoint.
claims.design_implication: Offer a tag on the creatine tub that fires a Shortcut doing a POST to the Go backend's /intake endpoint (works without any Swift code). Keep an in-app one-tap and a Watch complication as the primary path.

claims.claim: HealthKit has toothbrushingEvent as a category type (HKCategoryTypeIdentifier.toothbrushingEvent), logged as start and end times of brushing sessions. I could not retrieve the Apple page, so details of metadata and write rules are unverified. Oral-B, Oclean Care and Philips Sonicare (app version 10.5.0 and newer; newer Philips Dental+ app) all advertise Apple Health sync. Which data types each writes was not stated in the sources. Sonicare sync needs a connected brush and the app in use. One user reported bulk backfills carry old timestamps with recent write times, which breaks incremental sync keyed on creation date. Quip was not checked.
claims.design_implication: Query HealthKit by sample start/end date, not by the anchored creation order, so back-filled sessions are not missed. Treat brushing from the toothbrush as the primary source if they own a smart brush, and keep a manual tap as the default so it works with a plain brush.

findings.recommended_approach: Treat labs as a private reference table plus informational nudges, not medical advice. Ingestion: (1) primary is PDF upload from Files or Share Sheet into the Go backend, where a vision LLM (Claude with PDF input) extracts rows into a strict schema (analyte, LOINC, value, unit, ref range, flag, collection date, lab). A mandatory review screen then lets the user confirm each row against the PDF page. (2) Secondary, behind a spike, is a small Swift plugin in the Flutter app that reads HKClinicalType.labResultsRecord and posts FHIR JSON; parse every coding and take effectiveDateTime as the date. Nudges: a hand-written rules table of at most around 8 markers (vitamin D, B12, ferritin, magnesium, plus a few lipids and glucose flags) that each produce a suggestion card with the reasoning, max dose, retest interval and 'talk to your doctor' flag. Adherence: own table; Huel and creatine are daily check-ins with a lock-screen/Watch one-tap, optional NFC tag firing a Shortcut POST, streak and points computed server-side with a grace rule. Brushing: manual morning/evening tap as the baseline, plus HealthKit ingestion of toothbrushingEvent when a smart brush app syncs, deduped by time window. Guardrails: persistent 'not medical advice' on every nudge screen; no dose recommendation above the ODS upper intake; always show the reference range from the PDF; out-of-range critical values (very high or low) display 'see a clinician' and never a supplement; no iron suggestion without ferritin and a doctor prompt; pregnancy, kidney disease, medications and existing supplements are collected in the profile checklist and suppress relevant cards; never let the LLM author the recommendation text or doses, and log the source row for every nudge.
alternatives: Manual entry only: type the 6-10 key values per test; zero extraction risk, but friction means it may not get used.
Apple Health 'Export All Health Data' zip: parse the FHIR JSON on the backend; no entitlement needed, but manual and heavy each time.
Deterministic per-lab PDF parsers (as in the family-health or LabKit projects): no LLM cost or hallucination, but brittle across layouts.
Skip lab nudges and use generic vitamin reminders only: lowest risk, much less personal.
Writing labs back into HealthKit: not viable since most analytes have no HK type.
cannot_do: Third-party apps cannot write Clinical Health Records; they are read-only.
Shortcuts cannot read clinical records.
HealthKit has no supplement or creatine type, and most lab analytes have no standard HealthKit quantity type.
Silent NFC tap-to-log from inside a custom app is not possible; it must go through a Shortcut, and lock-state behavior was not verified.
I could not verify NIH ODS dosing figures directly (403), the Apple toothbrushingEvent page, Quest brush support, or whether the clinical-records entitlement works through TestFlight.
The app cannot diagnose or prescribe; it can only give informational, low-risk suggestions.
open_questions_for_user: Which lab or health system did each of you use (Quest, Labcorp, Kaiser or another Epic system), and is it connected in the Health app's Health Records?
Do you have electric toothbrushes (Oral-B, Sonicare, Oclean, Quip), and do either of you use a plain brush?
Do you take any medications or other supplements, or have kidney, iron, or thyroid conditions, pregnancy plans, or similar? These would suppress some nudges.
Are you comfortable with sending lab PDFs to a cloud LLM (Claude API), or do you want extraction local only?
Do you want a small Swift module in the Flutter app for HealthKit clinical records, given the entitlement/TestFlight risk?

Do you want an NFC tag on the tubs, or is a notification/Watch one-tap enough?

verdicts.claim: 1. Lab results are read-only HKClinicalRecord samples (labResultsRecord) with fhirResource holding FHIR Observation JSON, LOINC-coded, readable by third parties with per-type permission.
verdicts.evidence: clinical-vitals-sync README (https://github.com/speckofthecosmos/clinical-vitals-sync) confirms FHIR Observation fields (code, effectiveDateTime, valueQuantity, component) and Epic stacking LOINC codings. The HKClinicalRecord API shape is stable and I found no iOS 26 change. I did not re-fetch the WWDC20 session.
verdicts.correction: None. The 'normally LOINC' wording is right, since coding is provider-dependent.

verdicts.claim: 2. Clinical records need the HealthKit capability with Clinical Health Records, plus the two Info.plist keys. A free team cannot use it. Apple reviews the entitlement only at App Review. TestFlight is unverified.
verdicts.evidence: https://newly.app/articles/health-records-entitlement confirms entitlement com.apple.developer.healthkit.access = [health-records], both usage-description keys, 'no pre-approval form', and review at submission. It also says a valid privacy policy URL is needed. It is silent on free teams and TestFlight. The README (https://github.com/speckofthecosmos/clinical-vitals-sync) states 'A free team can't use it' and does not mention TestFlight. TestFlight remains unverified.
verdicts.correction: Add that a privacy policy URL is expected. Treat 'works on TestFlight external or internal builds' as unknown. Internal TestFlight testing on Nick's own paid team most likely works, but this is an inference. Keep the spike.

verdicts.claim: 3. Apple Health Records only has data if a provider is connected. Labcorp and Quest joined. Current status is unverified. Epic exports are multi-coded, and effectiveDateTime must be used because the HealthKit start date is ingestion time.
verdicts.evidence: The README (https://github.com/speckofthecosmos/clinical-vitals-sync) confirms both the multi-coding behavior and the startDate vs effectiveDateTime point. I did not re-verify the Labcorp and Quest participation pages. Those are 2018-era news items, so current status stays unverified.
verdicts.correction: None. Keep 'current institution support unverified' and have Nick check the Health app's Health Records provider search for his and Nadia's actual providers before investing in the plugin.

verdicts.claim: 4. Shortcuts cannot read clinical records. Most analytes have no HealthKit quantity type. Manual alternative is Export All Health Data zip with FHIR JSON.
verdicts.evidence: The README (https://github.com/speckofthecosmos/clinical-vitals-sync) says Shortcuts' Find Health Samples covers only standard types, and that the export zip holds FHIR JSON under apple_health_export/clinical-records/.
verdicts.correction: None.

verdicts.claim: 5. PDF extraction: LLM vision or deterministic parsers; vendors do LOINC and UCUM normalization; one hand-audit found 4 of 88 rows wrong; no peer-reviewed benchmark.
verdicts.evidence: I did not re-fetch these vendor or GitHub sources (sensible.so, volohealth, LabLedger PR 4). The claim is a survey of anecdotes, and nothing I saw contradicts it.
verdicts.correction: Keep as anecdotal. The mandatory per-row review screen in the recommendation is the right mitigation regardless.

verdicts.claim: 6. Supplement mappings and limits: vitamin D UL 4000 IU/day; magnesium supplement UL 350 mg/day; B12, iron guidance.
verdicts.evidence: The ODS fact sheets returned 403 again (https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/VitaminD-HealthProfessional/). A search confirmed magnesium: 350 mg/day UL applies to supplemental magnesium only (not food) and is separate from the 420 mg Daily Value; it is debated (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10509448/ argues for re-evaluation, an advocacy view). The vitamin D 4000 IU figure is not confirmed by any source I retrieved. It matches my background knowledge of the NIH/IOM UL.
verdicts.correction: Magnesium 350 mg is confirmed as supplement-only. Vitamin D 4000 IU stays background-knowledge. Rather than hardcode doses, have the rules table cite the ODS URL per marker, and have a human (Nick) verify each number once against the fact sheets in a browser.

verdicts.claim: 7. Creatine: ISSN 2017 position finds no compelling evidence of renal harm in healthy people; serum creatinine rises predictably; evidence in kidney disease is limited.
verdicts.evidence: I did not retrieve the primary paper or either secondary source. This matches my background knowledge of the ISSN position stand.
verdicts.correction: Treat as plausible. The creatinine-rise point matters operationally. If bloodwork ingestion flags high creatinine or low eGFR for a creatine user, show an informational note ('creatine can raise creatinine') plus 'see a clinician', not a supplement suggestion.

verdicts.claim: 8. HealthKit has no dietary supplement type for creatine or Huel; nutrition types exist; supplement adherence is app-owned data.
verdicts.evidence: The claim is incomplete for iOS 26. HealthKit gained a Medications API at WWDC25 (HKUserAnnotatedMedication, HKMedicationConcept, HKMedicationDoseEvent; https://developer.apple.com/videos/play/wwdc2025/321/, https://developer.apple.com/documentation/healthkit/hkuserannotatedmedication.md). Separately, the quantity types for individual nutrients (e.g. dietaryProtein, dietaryVitaminD, dietaryEnergyConsumed) do exist.
verdicts.correction: There is still no dedicated creatine or Huel supplement type, and app-owned adherence data remains the right primary design. But iOS 26 gives a read path: the app may read HKMedicationDoseEvent for user-tracked vitamins or supplements (if the user adds creatine in Health's Medications), as an optional dedupe source. Add that to the spike list. Huel can still be logged as nutrition quantity samples.

verdicts.claim: Recommendation item: HealthKit toothbrushingEvent ingestion when a smart brush app syncs.

verdicts.correction: Keep the manual tap as the baseline. Ingestion is a bonus and depends on Nick and Nadia owning a brush whose app writes to Health. Ask them which brush they have.
